cards.q: What is software testing, and why do we need it?
cards.a: Testing is checking a product against requirements and user expectations to find defects and give the team information about its quality. We need it to reduce risk: a bug found in production costs much more than one found early, and testing gives stakeholders the data to decide whether to release. It doesn't prove there are no bugs; it shows where they are.
cards.d:
Testing is the process of evaluating a product to find defects and to check that it meets requirements and user expectations. Its purpose is to give the team information about quality so they can make release decisions, and to reduce the risk of failures in production, which cost far more to fix than bugs found early.

  • Avoid "making sure software works": testing can't prove that (principle #1).
  • Explain the why: risk, cost of late bugs, release decisions.
  • Diagnosing the cause is debugging (developer). Testing finds the failure.

cards.q: What are the goals (objectives) of testing?
cards.a: To find defects and failures; to check that requirements are met and that the product does what users need; to prevent defects by reviewing requirements early; to build confidence in the product's quality; and to give stakeholders information to make decisions, like whether to release. Overall, to reduce the risk of problems in production.
cards.d: ISTQB also lists: evaluating work products (requirements, stories, code) and meeting contractual, legal or regulatory requirements. Goals change with context: in development the aim is to find as many defects as possible; in acceptance testing it is to confirm the system works as expected.

cards.q: QA vs QC vs testing?
cards.a: They nest: QA contains QC, and QC contains testing. QA is about the process and prevents defects. QC is about the product and detects defects. Testing is one QC activity: running or reviewing the software to find defects.
cards.d:
• Quality Assurance: process-oriented and preventive. Sets up processes, standards and reviews across the whole SDLC so defects don't appear. Examples: requirement reviews, standards, Definition of Done, test strategy.
  • Quality Control: product-oriented and detective. Checks the actual product for defects: inspecting the built product against the quality bar.
  • Testing: a QC activity: executing or reviewing the product to find defects.

Restaurant analogy: QA = hygiene rules and recipes; QC = inspecting dishes before they go out; testing = tasting this soup.

Interview line: "My title is QA engineer, but most daily work is QC and testing. I touch QA when I review requirements or help define the DoD."

cards.q: Verification vs validation? If the spec is good, why validate at all?
cards.a: Verification asks "are we building the product right?": does it match the spec? Validation asks "are we building the right product?": does it meet the user's real need? You can pass verification and still fail validation. The spec is the analyst's best understanding of the need, but it's never complete or perfectly correct. Validation checks the product against the real need, through requirements review, UAT and exploratory testing, so gaps in the spec don't reach users.
cards.d:
• Verification example: spec says password 8–20 characters; 7 is rejected, 8 accepted.
  • Validation example: the rule works, but users keep getting locked out because it's confusing.
  • Memory hook: verification = matches the document; validation = matches the need.
  • Failing validation while passing verification is the absence-of-errors fallacy.

The spec is a translation, and translations lose things:

  • Users often can't say what they need until they see the product.
  • The analyst works from assumptions, and some are wrong.
  • Specs rarely cover edge cases, error handling or usability.
  • Needs change while the product is built.

Validation activities that bypass the document: requirements review, UAT / alpha / beta, exploratory and usability testing. In Agile, with thin specs, the tester validates directly with the PO.

cards.q: Error vs defect vs failure?
cards.a: An error is a human mistake. It creates a defect (a bug) in the code or a document. When that code runs, the defect can cause a failure: behaviour you can observe that differs from what's expected.
cards.d:
Error (mistake) → Defect (bug, fault) → Failure, an observable deviation from expected behaviour. A developer types < instead of <= (error); the wrong check is in the code (defect); an 18-year-old user is rejected (failure).

  • Not every defect causes a failure: dead code, or an input that never happens.
  • Not every failure comes from a defect; failures can also come from the environment: full disk, network outage, bad config.
  • What a tester sees is the failure; the developer finds the defect.

cards.q: Name the 7 principles of testing, with examples.
cards.a: 1. Testing shows the presence of defects, not their absence. 2. Exhaustive testing is impossible. 3. Early testing saves time and money. 4. Defects cluster together. 5. Pesticide paradox, or tests wear out. 6. Testing is context dependent. 7. Absence-of-errors fallacy. Three examples. Defect clustering: most bugs sit in a few modules, so when checkout has given ten bugs I test checkout harder. Pesticide paradox: the same regression suite stops finding bugs, so I keep adding and changing tests. Absence-of-errors fallacy: a bug-free feature nobody can figure out how to use is still a failed product.
cards.d:
What each principle means:

  1. You can prove a bug exists, never that none exist.
  2. Infinite inputs, so we use risk and prioritisation: choose tests by risk and technique.
  3. Shift left: a bug in requirements costs a conversation; in production, a hotfix.
  4. A few modules hold most bugs, so test harder there.
  5. ISTQB 4.0 calls it "tests wear out": repeating the same tests stops finding new bugs; update them.
  6. A bank app, a game and a pacemaker are tested differently.
  7. A bug-free product that doesn't meet user needs is still a failure.

Groups to remember: what testing can't do (1, 2, 7); where and when (3, 4, 6); keep tests fresh (5). Naming 4–5 confidently is a strong answer.

Say all seven first, then explain. Practise writing the list from memory until it takes under 30 seconds.

cards.q: Severity vs priority, with examples where they do not match.
cards.a: Severity is how badly a bug affects the system; QA sets it. Priority is how urgently the business needs it fixed; the PM or PO sets it. High severity, low priority: a crash in a legacy report one person opens once a year. Low severity, high priority: the company name misspelled on the home page.
cards.d:
• Severity is technical impact on the system. Levels: Blocker, Critical, Major, Minor, Trivial.
  • Priority is business urgency of the fix: High, Medium, Low. QA can propose it.
  • High severity, low priority: app crashes in a rarely used legacy report that only one internal user opens once a year.
  • Low severity, high priority: the company name is misspelled on the home page, or the logo is wrong before a marketing launch.
  • High/High: users can't pay at checkout.
  • Low/Low: a 2-pixel misalignment on the About page.
  • Give both directions; interviewers often ask.
  • Your PayPal example (broken, but 0.5% of users) works. If challenged: "It depends on business context; the PO decides priority. My job is to report severity accurately and give them the data."

cards.q: Describe the bug life cycle.
cards.a: QA files it as New. The lead triages it and assigns a developer (Assigned/Open). The developer works on it (In Progress) and fixes it (Fixed). QA retests it: if it's gone, it's Verified and Closed; if not, it's Reopened. It can also be Rejected, a Duplicate, Cannot reproduce, or Deferred.
cards.d:
New → Assigned → Open / In Progress → Fixed (Resolved) → Ready for retest → Retest → Verified/Closed, or Reopened if it still reproduces.

StatusWho
NewQA files the report
Assigned / OpenLead or PM triages, sets priority
In ProgressDeveloper
Fixed / ResolvedDeveloper deploys the fix
RetestQA
Verified → ClosedQA
ReopenedQA, if it still reproduces

Side exits: Rejected / Not a bug, Duplicate, Cannot reproduce, Deferred (fix later), Won't fix.

  • The tester opens the bug and the tester closes it.
  • The exact statuses depend on the project's Jira workflow, so on a new project you ask for it.

cards.q: What is the STLC?
cards.a: STLC is the Software Testing Life Cycle: the phases that testing goes through. First comes requirement analysis, then test planning, then test design, where we write test cases and prepare data. After that we set up the environment, then execute the tests, report bugs and retest. The last phase is test closure, with a report and lessons learned. Each phase has its own entry and exit criteria.
cards.d: Software Testing Life Cycle: requirement analysis → test planning → test design (cases, data) → environment setup → test execution (and bug reporting, retesting) → test closure (report, lessons learned). Each phase has entry and exit criteria.

cards.q: What are entry and exit criteria?
cards.a: Entry criteria are the conditions we need before we can start testing. For example, the build is deployed to the test environment, the smoke test passed, requirements are available and test data is ready. Exit criteria are the conditions to stop testing. For example, all planned high-priority cases are executed, there are no open Blocker or Critical bugs, the pass rate is 95%, or the deadline is reached and the PM accepts the remaining risks.
cards.d: Entry criteria: conditions to start testing, e.g. build deployed to test env, smoke test passed, requirements available, test data ready. Exit criteria: conditions to stop, e.g. all planned high-priority cases executed, no open Blocker/Critical bugs, 95% pass rate, deadline reached with risks accepted by PM.

cards.q: Static vs dynamic testing?
cards.a: Static testing checks work products without running the code: reviews of requirements, designs and code, plus static analysis tools. Dynamic testing runs the software and checks its behaviour. Static testing finds defects earlier and cheaper, including defects in requirements; dynamic testing finds failures that only appear at run time.
cards.d:
Static: without running code: reviews of requirements, design, code; static analysis tools (linters). Finds defects earliest and cheapest. Dynamic: running the software and checking its behaviour.

Also in the practice scope: cause-effect graphing, a diagram of causes (input conditions) and effects (results) that is then converted into a decision table.

cards.q: What is the psychology of testing? Tester vs developer mindset?
cards.a: A developer's mindset is to build and to show that the code works; a tester's is to question it and look for where it fails. People also suffer from confirmation bias: authors find it hard to see their own mistakes, which is why independent testing helps. Because finding bugs can feel like criticism, a tester reports them neutrally and factually, about the product and never about the person.
cards.d:
• Good practice: start from shared goals ("we both want a good release"), describe facts, confirm the other person understood.
  • Levels of independence: the author tests their own work → a colleague → a separate test team → an outside organisation.

cards.q: What is the tester's code of ethics?
cards.a: ISTQB has a code of ethics for testers. In short: act in the public interest, act in the best interests of the client and employer, keep professional standards for the product, keep your judgement honest and independent, and treat colleagues fairly while continuing to learn. In practice it means: don't hide bugs, don't misuse confidential data or test data, and report results truthfully.
cards.d: The eight points: Public, Client and employer, Product, Judgment, Management, Profession, Colleagues, Self.

cards.q: What makes a good tester?
cards.a: I think a good tester has attention to detail, curiosity and a critical "what if" mindset. A good tester also writes clearly, because bug reports must be easy to understand, and understands the business and the user. And a good tester is diplomatic: we report problems in the product, not in people.
cards.d: Attention to detail, curiosity, a critical "what if" mindset, clear written communication (bug reports), understanding of the business and the user, and diplomacy: you report problems in the product, not in people.

cards.q: What is the SDLC and its phases?
cards.a: SDLC is the Software Development Life Cycle: the stages a product goes through. The phases are requirements gathering and analysis, then design of the architecture and UI, then implementation, which is coding, then testing, deployment and maintenance. A methodology or model defines how these stages are ordered and repeated.
cards.d: Software Development Life Cycle: the stages a product goes through: requirements gathering and analysis → design (architecture, UI) → implementation (coding) → testing → deployment → maintenance. A methodology/model defines how these stages are ordered and repeated.

cards.q: Explain Waterfall. Pros, cons, biggest weakness for a tester?
cards.a: Waterfall runs the phases strictly in sequence: requirements, design, coding, testing, release. Each phase starts when the previous one is signed off. It's predictable and well documented, so it suits fixed requirements. The cons are that changes to requirements are hard and the customer sees the product only at the end. The biggest weakness for QA is that testing comes late, so a requirements mistake is found only after it's been built, when it's most expensive to fix.
cards.d:
• Pros: simple to manage, predictable budget and timeline, thorough documentation.
  • Cons: testing happens late, so bugs are expensive; changes to requirements are hard (changes mid-way are painful); the customer sees the product only at the end.
  • Fits: small or fixed-scope projects, regulated domains (medical, government) with stable requirements.
  • Give it credit in the interview: say the pros and where it fits, not only the weakness.

cards.q: Explain the V-model.
cards.a: A sequential model where each development phase has a matching test level, planned at the same time: requirements with acceptance testing, system design with system testing, architecture with integration testing, module design with unit testing. Testers get involved from day one.
cards.d:
A Waterfall variant where every development phase on the left has a matching test level on the right:

DevelopmentTest level
Business requirementsAcceptance testing
System requirements / designSystem testing
Architecture (high-level design)Integration testing
Module (low-level) designUnit testing
Coding at the bottom

The V shape:

Requirements ─────────────► Acceptance testing
   System design ───────► System testing
      Architecture ───► Integration testing
         Module design ► Unit testing
                 \   /
                 Coding
  • Key point: test planning and design start in parallel with each development phase, not after coding.
  • Benefit: test design and requirement review start early (shift-left).
  • Limit: tests still run after coding; changes are still hard.
  • Memory hook: every step down the left gets a matching test on the right.

cards.q: Iterative vs incremental model?
cards.a: Incremental means building the product piece by piece: each increment adds a finished part, like login first, then the catalogue, then payments. Iterative means building a rough version of the whole thing and refining it in repeated cycles. Agile does both: each sprint adds new pieces and improves existing ones.
cards.d:
Incremental: the product is built and delivered in pieces (increments), each adding functionality. Iterative: the product is refined in repeated cycles, each going through design-build-test.

Painting analogy: incremental = finish the picture one square at a time; iterative = sketch the whole picture, then add detail in each pass.

Be ready to compare all five models: Waterfall, V-model, iterative, incremental, spiral: flow, when testing happens, how change is handled.

cards.q: Explain the Spiral model. When is it used?
cards.a: The Spiral model is a risk-driven, iterative model. The project goes around a spiral several times, and each loop has four steps: set objectives, analyse and reduce risks (often with a prototype), develop and test, then review with the customer and plan the next loop. It suits large, expensive, high-risk projects where requirements aren't clear upfront. It is costly and needs risk-analysis expertise, so it's overkill for small projects.
cards.d:
Each loop of the spiral goes through planning → risk analysis → engineering (build + test) → customer evaluation:

Loop stepWhat happens
1. PlanningObjectives, alternatives, constraints
2. Risk analysisIdentify risks, build a prototype to reduce them
3. EngineeringDesign, code, test this version
4. EvaluationCustomer reviews, next loop is planned
  • Pros: risks handled early, customer sees prototypes, changes are possible.
  • Cons: expensive, complex to manage, hard to say when it ends.
  • Author: Barry Boehm, 1986. Each loop makes the product more complete.

cards.q: What is the Prototype model / RAD?
cards.a: The Prototype model means we first build a quick mock-up to clarify unclear requirements with the customer, and then we build the real product. RAD is Rapid Application Development. It uses short timeboxes, reusable components and heavy user involvement, and it uses prototypes instead of long specifications.
cards.d: Prototype: build a quick mock-up to clarify unclear requirements with the customer, then build the real thing. RAD (Rapid Application Development): short timeboxes, reusable components, heavy user involvement, prototypes instead of long specs.

cards.q: Agile vs Waterfall?
cards.a: Waterfall goes through sequential phases, and Agile works in short iterations. In Waterfall the requirements are fixed upfront; in Agile they evolve and changes are welcome. In Waterfall testing is a separate phase at the end; in Agile it is continuous, in every sprint. The Waterfall customer sees the result only at the end, but in Agile the customer gives feedback every iteration. Waterfall has heavy documentation; Agile keeps just enough.
cards.d:
WaterfallAgile
FlowSequential phasesShort iterations
RequirementsFixed upfrontEvolve, welcomed changes
TestingSeparate phase at the endContinuous, every sprint
CustomerSees result at the endFeedback every iteration
DocsHeavyJust enough

cards.q: Which model would you choose for a project? When Waterfall or V-model over Agile?
cards.a: It depends on the project's traits. With unclear or changing requirements and a need for fast feedback, I'd choose Agile. I'd choose Waterfall or the V-model when requirements are fixed and well understood, when the customer can't give frequent feedback, or when regulation demands full documentation and traceability. Example: firmware for a medical infusion pump. Requirements come from regulations, every requirement must trace to a test, and auditors need the documents, so the V-model fits.
cards.d:
Reason from the project's traits: stable, fully known requirements and strict regulation → Waterfall/V-model. Unclear or changing requirements, need for fast feedback → Agile (Scrum/Kanban). Huge, risky, expensive → Spiral. Customer unsure what they want → start with a prototype. Say the trade-off out loud; there's no single right answer.

  • Typical domains: medical devices, automotive, aviation, banking core systems, fixed-price government contracts.
  • Hardware pushes toward sequential planning: you can't ship a new circuit board every two weeks.

Drop filler like "there are other cases too": name one or stop.

cards.q: What are the 4 values of the Agile Manifesto?
cards.a: The Agile Manifesto has four values. First, individuals and interactions over processes and tools. Second, working software over comprehensive documentation. Third, customer collaboration over contract negotiation. Fourth, responding to change over following a plan. The items on the right still have value, but we value the items on the left more.
cards.d:
1. Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
  2. Working software over comprehensive documentation
  3. Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
  4. Responding to change over following a plan

The items on the right still have value; the left is valued more.

cards.q: Name some of the 12 principles behind the Agile Manifesto.
cards.a: Satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery. Welcome changing requirements, even late. Deliver working software frequently. Business people and developers work together daily. Working software is the main measure of progress. Keep a sustainable pace. And the team regularly reflects on how to become more effective.
cards.d: The rest: build projects around motivated people; face-to-face conversation; continuous attention to technical excellence; simplicity; self-organising teams. Naming five or six is plenty.

cards.q: Advantages and disadvantages of Agile?
cards.a: Advantages: working software is delivered early and often, changes are welcome, the customer gives feedback every iteration, and bugs are found early because testing is continuous. Disadvantages: the final scope, cost and date are hard to predict; documentation is thin; it needs an involved customer and a mature, self-organising team; and scope can creep.
cards.d: Also a con: harder to scale to many teams and awkward with fixed-price contracts.

cards.q: Describe Scrum: roles, events, artifacts.
cards.a: Three roles: the Product Owner, who decides what gets built and in what order; the Scrum Master, a coach who removes blockers; and the Developers, everyone who builds the product, including QA. Five events: the Sprint, Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Retrospective. Three artifacts: the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog and the Increment, which must meet the Definition of Done.
cards.d:
• Product Owner: owns and orders the Product Backlog, maximises value.
  • Scrum Master: coaches the team on Scrum, removes impediments, facilitates.
  • Developers: everyone who builds the increment, including QA.

Events: Sprint (fixed 1–4 weeks, usually 2, a container for everything), Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum (15 min), Sprint Review (demo: show the product to stakeholders), Sprint Retrospective (improve the process, how the team works).

Artifacts: Product Backlog (Product Goal), Sprint Backlog (Sprint Goal), Increment (Definition of Done).

  • Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity, not an event, and it's where QA adds the most value.
  • Say explicitly: there's no separate tester role in Scrum; QA is one of the Developers.

cards.q: What happens at the Daily Scrum? 2017 vs 2020 Scrum Guide?
cards.a: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute daily meeting where the team inspects progress toward the Sprint Goal and plans the next 24 hours. The classic three questions are: what did I do yesterday, what will I do today, and do I have any impediments. The 2017 guide names the roles Product Owner, Scrum Master and Development Team; the 2020 guide renamed the team to Developers, dropped the three questions as mandatory, and added the Product Goal.
cards.d: Some companies still use the 2017 guide's wording ("Development Team", "roles"), so know it and mention you know the 2020 changes.

cards.q: What does a QA engineer do during a sprint?
cards.a: Three things. Before coding, I ask questions about stories to find gaps early. During the sprint, I test each story as soon as it's done, report bugs and check the fixes. At the end, I run regression to make sure nothing old broke before the release. Ask early, test continuously, check before release.
cards.d:
• Refinement: reviews stories, asks questions, makes acceptance criteria testable ("What if the promo code is expired?").
  • Planning: estimates testing effort.
  • Writes test cases/checklists while devs code; prepares test data.
  • Tests stories as soon as they're done, reports and retests bugs.
  • Runs regression before the end of the sprint/release.
  • Daily: says what's tested, what's blocked, which bugs are critical.
  • Review: takes part, sometimes demos.
  • Retro: raises process problems ("stories reach QA on the last day").

cards.q: Scrum vs Kanban?
cards.a: Scrum works in fixed sprints with set roles and events. Kanban has no sprints: tasks flow continuously across a board, and the main rule is a WIP limit on each column so work doesn't pile up. Kanban suits support teams where tasks arrive unpredictably.
cards.d:
ScrumKanban
CadenceFixed sprintsContinuous flow
RolesPO, SM, DevelopersNo required roles
ChangeSprint scope protected; changes wait for next sprintChange anytime
LimitWork per sprintWIP limit: tasks per column
MetricsVelocity, burndownLead time, cycle time, CFD

Kanban suits support and maintenance work with unpredictable incoming tasks.

Note: the key Kanban rule is how many tasks can be in a stage (WIP limit), not how long each stage takes.

cards.q: What is XP (Extreme Programming)?
cards.a: XP, or Extreme Programming, is an Agile method that focuses on engineering practices. The main ones are pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, small frequent releases and refactoring. It also uses simple design, collective code ownership, coding standards, an on-site customer and a sustainable pace.
cards.d: An Agile method focused on engineering practices: pair programming, test-driven development (TDD), continuous integration, small frequent releases, refactoring, simple design, collective code ownership, coding standards, an on-site customer, sustainable pace.

cards.q: What is a user story? What makes a good one?
cards.a: A short requirement from the user's point of view: "As a [role], I want [goal], so that [benefit]." It's kept brief on purpose; the details go into acceptance criteria, which QA helps make testable. A good story follows INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable.
cards.d:
Acceptance criteria are often written in Gherkin: Given context, When action, Then result.

Example: As a registered customer, I want to save items to a wishlist, so that I can buy them later.

Acceptance criterion: Given I'm logged in, when I click the heart icon, then the item appears in my wishlist.

Use case vs user story: a use case is detailed (actor, main flow, alternatives, errors); a user story is short (who, what, why) plus acceptance criteria.

cards.q: Definition of Ready vs Definition of Done?
cards.a: The Definition of Ready says what a story needs before entering a sprint: a clear description, acceptance criteria, designs and an estimate. The Definition of Done is a checklist the whole team agrees on that every story must meet to count as done. For example: code reviewed, tested, no critical bugs open, deployed to stage. It differs from acceptance criteria, which are specific to one story.
cards.d:
DoR: when a story is ready to be taken into a sprint: clear description, acceptance criteria, designs attached, estimated, dependencies known. DoD: when an increment is done: code reviewed, tests passed, no open critical bugs, acceptance criteria met, docs updated, deployed to staging.

  • Don't call it "self-explanatory" in an interview; just answer.

cards.q: Other Agile frameworks you have heard of?
cards.a: Yes, I have heard of several. Lean is about eliminating waste. Scrumban combines Scrum with a Kanban board and WIP limits. SAFe and LeSS are frameworks for scaling Agile across many teams. I also know the names FDD and DSDM.
cards.d: Lean (eliminate waste), Scrumban (Scrum + Kanban board/WIP limits), SAFe and LeSS (scaling Agile across many teams), FDD, DSDM.

cards.q: What are the levels of testing?
cards.a: Four, from smallest to biggest. Unit testing checks one piece of code alone, usually by developers. Integration testing checks that pieces work together. System testing checks the whole product end to end against requirements. Acceptance testing checks that it meets business needs, for example UAT by real users.
cards.d:
1. Unit / component: smallest pieces in isolation, usually by developers.
  2. Integration: interaction between components or systems (component integration, system integration, e.g. with a payment provider). Approaches: big bang, top-down (uses stubs), bottom-up (uses drivers), sandwich.
  3. System: the whole product end-to-end against requirements, in a production-like environment.
  4. Acceptance: does it meet business needs: UAT (users), alpha (in-house), beta (real users outside), operational (OAT), contractual/regulatory.

Memory hook: piece → pieces together → whole product → does the customer accept it. They match the right side of the V-model.

cards.q: Functional vs non-functional testing?
cards.a: Functional testing checks what the system does: does each feature work according to requirements? Non-functional testing checks how well it does it: performance, usability, security, compatibility, accessibility. On a login page, functional is that a correct password logs you in; non-functional is that login takes under 1 second.
cards.d:
Functional: checks what the system does against functional requirements (login works, total is calculated correctly).

Non-functional: checks how well it does it: performance (load, stress, spike, endurance/soak, volume, scalability), usability, security, compatibility (cross-browser, cross-platform), reliability, recovery, installability, localization, accessibility.

On one login page: functional = "a correct password logs you in"; non-functional = "login takes under 1 second", "the password is encrypted", "it works in Safari".

cards.q: What types of non-functional testing do you know?
cards.a: Performance testing, with load, stress, spike, endurance and volume testing. Usability testing: is it easy and clear to use. Security testing: is data protected and access controlled. Compatibility testing: browsers, operating systems, devices. Reliability and recovery testing: does it run without failures and recover after a crash. Installation testing. Localization and internationalization testing. And accessibility testing for people with disabilities.
cards.d:
One line each:

TypeQuestion it answers
LoadDoes it cope with the expected number of users?
StressWhere does it break, and how does it recover?
VolumeDoes it cope with a large amount of data?
ScalabilityDoes adding resources handle more load?
UsabilityCan users reach their goal easily?
SecurityCan someone get or change data they shouldn't?
CompatibilityDoes it work across browsers, OSes, devices?
Recovery / failoverWhat happens after a crash or lost connection?
InstallationInstall, update, uninstall cleanly?
LocalizationTranslation, dates, currency, RTL correct?
AccessibilityUsable with a screen reader or keyboard only?

cards.q: Performance vs load vs stress testing?
cards.a: Performance testing is the umbrella; load and stress testing are both types of it. Load testing checks behaviour under the expected load, up to the normal peak. Stress testing pushes beyond it until the system breaks, to find the breaking point and see how it fails and recovers.
cards.d:
• Load example: 1,000 concurrent users.
  • Spike: sudden jump in users.
  • Endurance (soak): normal load for a long time (hours), to catch memory leaks.
  • Tools: JMeter, k6, Gatling, LoadRunner.

Elevator rated for 8: load test = put 8 people in; stress test = keep adding people until it refuses to move, and check it fails safely.

cards.q: Smoke vs sanity testing?
cards.a: Smoke testing is wide and shallow: a quick check of the main functions on every new build, to see if it's testable at all. Sanity testing is narrow and focused: a quick check of one changed area after a fix, to confirm it makes sense to continue.
cards.d:
Smoke: a quick, broad, shallow check of the most critical functions of a new build (app opens, login, main flow) to decide if it's stable enough for further testing. Also called build verification testing.

Sanity: a quick, narrow, deep check of one specific area after a fix or small change, to confirm it works and it's reasonable to continue.

  • Smoke starts after the build is deployed; "does the build compile" is CI's job.
  • In practice, teams sometimes use the two terms loosely.

cards.q: Re-testing vs regression? Smoke vs regression?
cards.a: Re-testing checks that a specific bug is fixed by repeating its steps. Regression checks that the fix, or any change, didn't break other features that worked before. Re-testing targets a known bug; regression looks for new side effects. Smoke testing is a quick check of the most critical functions on a new build, to decide whether it's stable enough to test further. Regression testing is broader: it re-checks existing features to make sure new changes didn't break anything that worked before.
cards.d:
Re-testing (ISTQB calls it confirmation testing): run the exact failed scenario again to confirm a specific bug is fixed.

Regression testing: check that recent changes (fixes, new features, config) didn't break existing functionality that worked before. Good candidate for automation.

Re-testing is planned for known bugs; regression looks for unexpected side effects. They usually happen together: re-test the fix, then run regression around it.

SmokeRegression
QuestionIs this build testable at all?Did changes break what worked?
DepthShallow, critical pathsBroad and deep
TimeMinutesHours or days, often automated

cards.q: What is change-related testing? Is regression a level or a type?
cards.a: Testing done because something in the product changed. It has two parts: confirmation testing, or re-testing, which checks that a fixed bug is really fixed; and regression testing, which checks that the change didn't break anything that worked before. Smoke and sanity checks on a new build are often grouped here too. Regression is a test type, a change-related one, not a level: it can be performed at any level, unit, integration or system.
cards.d: White-box testing is based on the code's structure and is mostly done by developers at the unit and integration levels.

cards.q: Black-box vs white-box vs grey-box?
cards.a: Black-box testing is done without looking at the code, from requirements and behaviour; it's what most QA engineers do. White-box testing uses knowledge of the code to cover its internal paths, usually by developers. Grey-box is in between, for example testing the UI while also checking the database or API.
cards.d:
Black-box: based on requirements and behaviour, no knowledge of code. White-box: based on internal structure and code (statement and branch coverage), usually developers. Grey-box: partial knowledge, e.g. a tester who checks the DB, reads logs or knows the API behind the UI.

Obvious questions still get asked; answer fast and confidently.

cards.q: Positive vs negative testing?
cards.a: Positive testing uses valid data and expected flows and checks that the system does what it should. Negative testing uses invalid data and unexpected actions and checks that the system handles them gracefully: a clear error, no crash and no corrupted data. I run positive tests first, because if the main path fails, the negative cases don't matter yet.
cards.d: Positive: valid data and expected flows: the system does what it should. Negative: invalid data and unexpected actions: the system handles them gracefully (clear error, no crash, no corrupted data). Run positive first; if the main path fails, negatives don't matter yet.

cards.q: Exploratory vs ad hoc vs monkey testing?
cards.a: Exploratory testing is learning, designing and executing tests at the same time, without scripted cases. It's guided by a charter and a timebox, and you take notes. It's great for finding unexpected bugs and for features with little documentation. Ad hoc testing is informal: no goal, no planning and no notes. Monkey testing is random input to see if the app crashes.
cards.d:
• Charter example: "Explore checkout with discount codes to find calculation errors."
  • Timebox: 30–90 minutes.
  • Ad hoc is not the same as exploratory: informal, no planning or documentation, no goal, notes or structure.
  • Monkey testing can be automated, e.g. Android's adb shell monkey.

cards.q: Alpha vs beta testing?
cards.a: Alpha testing is acceptance testing inside the company, done by internal users or QA before the product is released to outsiders. Beta testing gives a near-final version to a limited group of real external users, who use it in their real environments. For mobile apps this is done through TestFlight or Google Play open or closed testing.
cards.d: Alpha: acceptance testing inside the company by internal users/QA, before release to outsiders. Beta: a near-final version given to a limited group of real external users in their real environments (TestFlight, Google Play open/closed testing).

cards.q: Localization vs internationalization?
cards.a: Internationalization, or i18n, means designing the product so it can support different languages and regions: no hard-coded strings, Unicode, flexible layouts, and date and currency formats. Localization, or l10n, means adapting the product for a specific locale: translation, local formats, right-to-left layout and cultural fit. So internationalization makes it possible, and localization does it for one locale.
cards.d: Internationalization (i18n): designing the product so it can support different languages and regions (no hard-coded strings, Unicode, flexible layouts, date/currency formats). Localization (l10n): adapting it for a specific locale: translation, formats, RTL layout, cultural fit.

cards.q: What is the test pyramid?
cards.a: The test pyramid is a guide for how to balance automated tests. The wide base is many fast, cheap unit tests. The middle layer is integration and API tests. The small top is a few slow, brittle UI end-to-end tests. The inverse shape is called the ice-cream cone, and it is an anti-pattern.
cards.d: A guide for automation balance: a wide base of fast, cheap unit tests; a middle layer of integration/API tests; a small top of slow, brittle UI end-to-end tests. The inverse ("ice-cream cone") is an anti-pattern.

cards.q: What documentation exists on a project? What test documentation do you know?
cards.a: Project documentation describes how the work is organised: the project plan, schedules, the test plan and reports. Product documentation describes the product itself: requirements and specifications, design and architecture documents, and user guides. Test documentation includes the test strategy, test plan, checklists, test cases, bug reports, the traceability matrix and test reports.
cards.d:
• Test policy / strategy: org- or project-level approach.
  • Test plan: scope, approach, resources, schedule, risks.
  • Checklist: list of things to check.
  • Test case: detailed steps with expected results; grouped into test suites.
  • Test scenario: high-level "what to test" (e.g. "user buys an item with a promo code").
  • Bug report.
  • Traceability matrix (RTM): maps requirements ↔ test cases ↔ bugs, shows coverage.
  • Test summary / progress report.

Documentation testing means reviewing these documents for clarity, completeness and consistency (static testing).

cards.q: What levels and types of requirements are there?
cards.a: Three levels. Business requirements say why the product is needed: the goals of the business. User requirements say what users must be able to do, written as use cases or user stories. Functional requirements say what the system must do to make that possible. Alongside those are non-functional requirements: quality attributes like performance and security, constraints, and business rules.
cards.d:
LevelExample
BusinessIncrease online sales by 20%
UserAs a customer I want to pay by card
FunctionalThe system validates the card number and shows an error if it is invalid
Non-functionalPayment confirmation appears within 3 seconds
Business ruleOrders over $500 need manager approval
ConstraintMust run on PostgreSQL

cards.q: How do you test requirements? What makes a requirement good?
cards.a: I review requirements before development starts. I check that each one is clear, complete, consistent with the others, and testable, meaning I could write a pass/fail test for it. When something is vague, like "the page should load fast", I ask the analyst to make it measurable. Catching that early is the cheapest bug fix there is.
cards.d:
"Testing requirements" means reviewing the document (static testing), not testing the product against it.

I check that each requirement is complete, correct, unambiguous, consistent (no contradictions), testable (measurable: "fast" → "loads in under 2 s"), feasible, traceable, and prioritised. "Lots of detail" isn't the criterion.

I ask the BA/PO questions about gaps, edge cases and error handling, and record the answers.

  • Ambiguous: "the password must be strong".
  • Incomplete: "users can delete their account" (what about their orders?).
  • Inconsistent: max 20 characters on page 3, 30 on page 7.
  • Not testable: "should load fast".

cards.q: Test plan vs test strategy? What does each contain?
cards.a: A test strategy is a high-level, long-lived document for the whole product or organisation: which test levels and types we use, the approach to automation, environments, tools, and how defects and reporting work. A test plan is for a specific project or release: what exactly is in and out of scope, who tests it and when, entry and exit criteria, the schedule and the risks. The strategy says how we test in general; the plan says what we'll do this time.
cards.d:
Test strategyTest plan
LevelOrganisation or productProject or release
ChangesRarelyEvery release
Written byQA lead or managerQA lead, with the team
AnswersHow do we test?What, who, when, with what?

Test plan sections: scope, approach, environments, entry and exit criteria, schedule, roles, risks, deliverables, tools. In small Agile teams the two are often one short document.

cards.q: What are the fields of a test case?
cards.a: A test case has an ID and a title, and sometimes the module or component. Then it has preconditions, test steps, test data and the expected result. It can also have postconditions, a priority, a link to the requirement or story, and the author. During execution we add the actual result, the status, which is Passed, Failed, Blocked or Skipped, and the environment or build.
cards.d: ID, title, (module/component), preconditions, test steps, test data, expected result, postconditions, priority, link to requirement/story, author, and during execution: actual result, status (Passed / Failed / Blocked / Skipped), environment/build.

cards.q: Checklist vs test case: when to use which?
cards.a: A checklist is a list of things to check, one line each, with no detailed steps. It's quick to write and flexible, but depends on the tester's knowledge. A test case has preconditions, exact steps and an expected result, so anyone can repeat it, but it takes longer to write and maintain. I'd use checklists for new features and test cases for critical flows and regression.
cards.d:
A checklist is also easy to maintain, but less reproducible. A test case is reproducible, good for newcomers, outsourcing and automation. Agile teams often use checklists for new features and test cases for critical regression.

Test case example: Title: login with valid credentials. Precondition: user test@mail.com exists. Steps: open /login, enter email and password, click Log in. Expected: redirected to the dashboard, name shown in the header.

Don't compare a test case to a user story: a story is a requirement; a test case verifies one. And never forget the expected result.

cards.q: What is a test suite?
cards.a: A test suite is a logical group of test cases that belong together. We can group them by feature, for example a Login suite with all the login test cases. We can group them by type, for example a Smoke suite or a Regression suite. Or we can group them by release.
cards.d: A logical group of test cases: by feature (Login suite), by type (Smoke suite, Regression suite) or by release.

cards.q: What does a good bug report contain?
cards.a: A summary that says what, where and when; the environment and build; preconditions; numbered steps to reproduce; the actual result; the expected result with a link to the requirement; severity and suggested priority; attachments like screenshots, video and logs; and how often it reproduces.
cards.d:
• Summary: What? Where? When? e.g. "Cart: total isn't updated after removing an item with a promo code applied".
  • Steps to reproduce: minimal, numbered, with test data.
  • Actual result vs Expected result (with reference to the requirement).
  • Environment: build/version, OS, browser + version, device, test env URL.
  • Severity, priority, component, attachments (screenshot, video, logs, HAR, console errors).
  • Reproducibility (always / 3 of 5).
  • One bug per report. Neutral tone.
  • QA owns severity; the PM or PO usually sets priority.

cards.q: What is a traceability matrix?
cards.a: A traceability matrix is a table that links each requirement to the test cases that cover it, and often to the bugs found as well. It shows coverage gaps, so I can see a requirement that has no tests. It helps to estimate the impact when a requirement changes. And it proves to stakeholders that everything was tested.
cards.d: A table that links each requirement to the test cases that cover it (and, often, the bugs found). It shows coverage gaps, helps estimate the impact of a requirement change, and proves to stakeholders that everything was tested.

cards.q: You join a new project. What are your first steps?
cards.a: First I get access to everything: Jira, docs, environments, test accounts. Then I learn the product by reading the docs and actually using it, and I learn the process: sprints, the bug workflow, who's responsible for what. I study existing test cases and open bugs, understand the architecture and environments, and start with something small, like running the regression suite. Throughout, I ask a lot of questions and note the answers.
cards.d:
1. Get access: task tracker (Jira), docs (Confluence), test environments and credentials, TMS, repository, VPN, chats.
  2. Understand the product: purpose, target users, business domain. Read requirements and specs, then use the product as a user.
  3. Understand the process: methodology, sprint length, ceremonies, bug workflow and statuses, DoD, release cycle, who to ask about what (PM, BA, devs, lead).
  4. Study existing QA artifacts: test plan, cases, checklists, known open bugs, release notes, test data.
  5. Understand the architecture: platforms (web/mobile), client-server, APIs, DB, third-party integrations, environments (dev/stage/prod).
  6. Ask questions and write down answers; draw a mind map of the product.
  7. Start small: run a smoke/regression with existing cases, then take my first tasks.

Also ask your lead what success looks like in your first month.

cards.q: What test environments exist on a project?
cards.a: Usually four. Dev is where developers integrate their code. Test, or QA, is where testers test new features. Staging, or pre-production, is a copy of production used for final regression and acceptance. Production is the live system real users use. Each has its own URL, database and test data.
cards.d: On a new project ask: which branch is deployed where, who deploys, where the test accounts and data are, and whether you may test on production (usually only read-only smoke checks).

cards.q: What is a release policy? What do you need to know about releases?
cards.a: The release policy is the team's rules for shipping: how often releases happen, when the code freeze is, how a release candidate is built and tested, who signs off, and how hotfixes and rollbacks work. As a tester I need to know the release calendar, what testing is required before sign-off, usually regression and smoke on the release candidate, and the scope of each iteration or release.
cards.d:
• Code freeze: no new features after this point, only fixes.
  • Release candidate: the build that ships if no blocker is found.
  • Hotfix: an urgent fix released outside the normal cycle.
  • Versioning is often major.minor.patch, e.g. 2.14.1.

cards.q: How do you interact with the team and with the client?
cards.a: With the team: daily meetings, the task tracker and chat. I ask the analyst about requirements, developers about implementation, and my lead about priorities, and I keep decisions written in the ticket. With the client: only through the agreed channels and people, usually via the PM or analyst unless I'm told otherwise. I'm polite, factual, I don't promise dates or scope on my own, and I never share internal problems or credentials.
cards.d: On day one, ask for the communication rules: who talks to the client, in which channel, in which language, and what the working hours and time zones are.

cards.q: There is no documentation. How do you test?
cards.a: I'd build my own understanding of how the product should work. I'd talk to the PO, developers and support, explore the product and any older versions, look at competitors, and rely on common standards. I'd write my assumptions down as checklists or a mind map and have the PO confirm them, so we end up with the documentation that was missing.
cards.d:
The real problem without docs: where do your expected results come from?

  • Talk to people: PO, BA, devs, support, other testers.
  • Explore the product (exploratory sessions), old versions, competitors, analytics.
  • Use common sense, platform guidelines (Apple HIG, Material) and standards.
  • Write down my assumptions as a checklist or mind map and get them confirmed by the PO. That becomes the first documentation.

Say "on a test environment", not "in prod": testing on production can touch real users' data.

cards.q: The task is unclear. What do you do?
cards.a: I don't guess silently. First I re-read the story and the related tickets. Then I ask the author, the BA or the PO, concrete questions. Ideally I ask in the ticket, so the answer is recorded. If the unclear task is blocking my work, I raise it at the daily meeting.
cards.d: I don't guess silently. I re-read the story and related tickets, then ask the author (BA/PO) concrete questions, ideally in the ticket so the answer is recorded. If it's blocking, I raise it at the daily.

cards.q: A developer says your bug is not a bug. What do you do?
cards.a: First I double-check the requirement and reproduce it again. If the spec supports me, I show the developer the requirement and evidence like a video or logs. If the spec is unclear, I bring in the PO or analyst, because it's a product decision, not a personal argument. Whatever we decide goes into the ticket. And if it works as designed but the design seems bad for users, I log it as an improvement.
cards.d:
Check the requirement and my steps again. If I'm right, I show the evidence: requirement reference, video, logs.

Your instinct, "one source of truth: the requirements", is exactly right.

cards.q: Release is tomorrow and you cannot test everything. What do you do?
cards.a: I'd use risk-based testing: smoke first, then critical business flows like payment, then new and changed features, then areas with a history of bugs. Most importantly, I'd tell the PM early, in writing, what won't be covered and what the risks are, so the go/no-go decision is informed. The rest gets tested after release.
cards.d:
Order: smoke → critical business flows → new/changed features → bug-prone areas → everything else. Run smoke + high-priority cases first.

Do not forget to communicate the risk. The release decision belongs to the PM or PO.

cards.q: You found a critical bug right before the release. What do you do?
cards.a: I report it immediately with full details and mark the severity. I also notify the PM or the lead directly, not just in Jira. Then the team decides what to do. There are three options: fix the bug and retest it, roll back the feature, or release with a known issue and a workaround.
cards.d: Report it immediately with full details, mark severity, and notify the PM/lead directly (not just in Jira). The team decides: fix and retest, roll back the feature, or release with a known issue and a workaround.

cards.q: How do you learn a new domain fast?
cards.a: I start with a glossary of the domain terms from the docs. Then I read the user scenarios and talk to the BA. I also look at competitor products, and I read support tickets and the production bug history. Those show what actually matters to users.
cards.d: Glossary from the docs, user scenarios, talk to the BA, look at competitor products, read support tickets and production bug history. Those show what actually matters to users.

cards.q: What test design techniques do you know? What categories are there?
cards.a: Three. Black-box techniques are based on requirements: equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision tables, state transition, use case testing and pairwise. White-box techniques are based on the code: statement coverage and decision coverage. Experience-based techniques rely on the tester's knowledge: error guessing, exploratory testing and checklist-based testing.
cards.d:
• Black-box (specification-based): equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision table, state transition, use-case testing, pairwise / combinatorial, cause-effect graph.
  • White-box (structure-based): statement coverage, branch/decision coverage, condition and path coverage.
  • Experience-based: error guessing, exploratory testing, checklist-based.

Be able to explain every technique named here with one example.

cards.q: Explain equivalence partitioning with an example.
cards.a: Splitting all possible inputs into groups the system should treat the same way, then testing one value from each group. For an Age field accepting 18 to 60: one valid value like 35, plus invalid groups such as below 18, above 60, letters, empty and decimals.
cards.d:
If one value in a class works, the others should too.

GroupValid?Test
18–60valid35
Below 18invalid10
Above 60invalid75
Not a numberinvalidabc
Emptyinvalid(nothing)
Decimalinvalid25.5

Other invalid classes: negative, special characters.

About 6 tests instead of 100. It's how you handle "exhaustive testing is impossible".

cards.q: Explain boundary value analysis with an example (Age 18 to 60).
cards.a: In boundary value analysis I test values exactly at the boundaries and right next to them. For an Age field that accepts 18 to 60, that is 17, 18, 60 and 61. Bugs tend to sit at the edges, like ">" instead of ">=". Together with equivalence partitioning, a middle value like 35 and invalid types like letters, that covers the field with very few tests.
cards.d:
Bugs gather at boundaries (< instead of <=). BVA complements EP: EP picks classes, BVA picks the edges of those classes.

  • 2-value BVA: 17, 18, 60, 61.
  • 3-value BVA: 17, 18, 19, 59, 60, 61.
  • "Below and above" means right next to the boundary; a value like 5 is EP, not BVA.

Apply it to lengths too: a 1–20 character field → 0, 1, 20, 21 characters.

cards.q: Explain the decision table technique (member AND promo code).
cards.a: A decision table lists every combination of conditions with the expected result for each; each column becomes a test case. I'd use it for business rules with several "if this and that" conditions, like discounts, shipping or login rules. It makes sure no combination is forgotten. For a discount that needs a member AND a valid promo code, that is four test cases: member with code, member without code, non-member with code, non-member without code. The discount applies only to a member with a valid code.
cards.d:
Used when the outcome depends on combinations of conditions. Rows: conditions and actions. Columns: rules (combinations). With n binary conditions you have up to 2ⁿ rules; impossible or irrelevant ones are collapsed.

Example: free shipping if the user is a member OR order ≥ $50.

R1R2R3R4
Member?YYNN
Order ≥ $50?YNYN
Free shipping✓✓✓✗

Each rule = at least one test case.

For the member AND promo code rule, I'd then expand "invalid code" into its own classes: expired, wrong, already used, empty, wrong letter case.

Combining techniques (a decision table, then EP inside one condition) shows method.

cards.q: Explain state transition testing (order statuses).
cards.a: State transition testing is for systems whose behaviour depends on the current state: I model the states and transitions, then test valid and invalid transitions. For an order going Created, Paid, Shipped, Delivered: first, every valid transition: the normal flow, plus cancelling from Created and from Paid, including the refund. Then the invalid ones: cancelling after shipping, skipping payment, going backwards, acting on a cancelled order. Those should all be blocked. I'd also check that the UI only offers the actions allowed in each state.
cards.d:
For systems whose behaviour depends on current state and history. We model states, events (inputs), transitions and sometimes guards, as a diagram or table, then test every valid transition and also invalid ones (they must be rejected).

  • Valid: Created→Paid→Shipped→Delivered; Created→Cancelled; Paid→Cancelled (refund!).
  • Invalid: cancel at Shipped or Delivered; Created→Shipped; Delivered→Paid; paying or shipping a cancelled order.
  • UI: a shipped order shows no Cancel button.

Example: ATM PIN. Wrong PIN once → 2nd attempt; twice → 3rd attempt; three times → card blocked. Correct PIN at any attempt → access. Test also: blocked card + correct PIN → still blocked.

cards.q: What is use case testing?
cards.a: A use case describes how an actor interacts with the system to reach a goal. It has a main success scenario, alternative flows and exception flows. In use case testing I write at least one test for the main flow and one for each alternative and exception flow. For "withdraw cash": the normal withdrawal, then choosing a receipt, then wrong PIN, insufficient funds and the ATM running out of cash.
cards.d: It is good at finding bugs in real end-to-end flows and at integration between steps. It was removed from the ISTQB v4.0 syllabus but is still commonly asked.

cards.q: What is pairwise testing?
cards.a: A way to reduce the number of combinations. Instead of testing every combination of parameters, I make sure every pair of values appears together at least once, because most bugs come from one parameter or from two interacting. For 3 browsers, 3 operating systems and 2 languages, that is 18 full combinations but only about 9 pairwise tests. Tools like PICT generate the set.
cards.d:
Combinatorial technique. Tools: PICT, pairwise.teremokgames.com, AllPairs.

Related: exhaustive testing means testing all combinations of inputs and preconditions. It is impossible except for trivial cases (principle #2), which is why techniques like pairwise, EP and BVA exist.

cards.q: Statement coverage vs decision (branch) coverage?
cards.a: Statement coverage measures the percentage of code statements, roughly lines, executed by tests. Decision coverage, also called branch coverage, measures the percentage of decision outcomes executed: both the true and the false side of every "if". 100% decision coverage guarantees 100% statement coverage, but not the other way round.
cards.d:
if (age >= 18) { allowed = true }
print(allowed)

One test with age = 20 runs every line: 100% statement coverage. But the false branch never ran: 50% decision coverage. Adding age = 10 gives 100% of both.

These are white-box techniques, mostly used by developers in unit tests. Their value: they show which code no test has touched.

cards.q: What are the experience-based techniques? Error guessing?
cards.a: Error guessing: using experience to predict where bugs are likely, like empty fields, zero, very long text, special characters or a double click on Submit. Exploratory testing: learning the product, designing and running tests at the same time, within a charter and a timebox. Checklist-based testing: testing against a list of high-level items or rules built from experience, without detailed steps.
cards.d:
They complement the formal techniques and are most useful when documentation is poor or time is short. Their weakness: coverage is hard to measure and depends on the tester.

Error guessing targets: empty fields, zero, negative numbers, very long strings, special characters and emoji, SQL/HTML in inputs, double click on submit, back button after payment, leading/trailing spaces, time zones and leap years.

cards.q: Practice: cinema ticket discounts. Design the tests.
cards.a: I'd combine techniques. A decision table for the rules: child or not, student or not, weekday or weekend, which gives the price for each combination, including a child who is also a student getting only the bigger discount. Boundary values on age: 11 and 12. Then equivalence classes for invalid input like a negative age or an empty one.
cards.d:
T1T2T3T4T5
