Student?–YYNN
Weekday?–YNYN
Price$5$8$10$10$10

"–" means the value doesn't matter. Ask the interviewer about gaps: is 12 a child? Is a holiday a weekday? Asking is part of the answer.

cards.q: What goes into a test plan?
cards.a: A test plan contains: scope (what will and won't be tested), approach (levels, types, manual or automated), environments and test data, entry and exit criteria, schedule, resources and roles, risks and how to handle them, deliverables, and tools.
cards.d:
Typical sections (IEEE 829 / ISO 29119-3): introduction and objectives; scope: features to test and not to test; approach: levels, types, techniques, manual/automation; test environments and test data; entry/exit criteria; suspension and resumption criteria (e.g. stop if the smoke fails); deliverables; schedule and milestones; resources and responsibilities; risks and mitigations; tools; approvals.

Memory hook: what, how, where, when, who, and what could go wrong.

cards.q: How do you estimate testing effort for a new feature?
cards.a: I break the work into tasks: analysing requirements, writing tests, preparing data, executing, re-testing bugs, regression, reporting. Then I estimate each one, using past similar features as a reference, and add a buffer for risks. For uncertain tasks I use a three-point estimate. In Scrum we'd estimate together in story points.
cards.d:
• WBS: break the work into small tasks (requirement analysis, test design, env setup, execution, retests, regression, reporting) and estimate each.
  • Three-point / PERT: E = (Optimistic + 4×Most likely + Pessimistic) / 6. e.g. (4 + 4×6 + 14) / 6 = 7 h.
  • Expert judgement / Wideband Delphi / planning poker: team estimates and converges.
  • Analogy / historical data: similar feature took X.
  • Ratio: testing ≈ 30–40% of dev effort (rough check).

Then add a risk buffer (10–20%) and state your assumptions.

WBS example, login page: requirements 0.5 h, test cases 2 h, data 0.5 h, execution 3 h, bugs and retests 1.5 h, regression 1 h, report 0.5 h → 9 h + 15% buffer ≈ 10–11 h.

"From experience" is a real technique (expert judgement), but name a method too.

cards.q: What estimation techniques do you know?
cards.a: Work breakdown structure: split the work into small tasks and estimate each. Three-point estimation, or PERT: combine optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values. Expert judgement and Wideband Delphi: experts estimate independently and converge. Estimation by analogy with similar past work. Planning poker with story points in Agile. And a ratio to development effort as a rough check.
cards.d:
Know at least four by name and be able to run one with numbers.

  • ISTQB v4.0 lists four: estimation based on ratios, extrapolation, Wideband Delphi, three-point.
  • Always add a buffer (10–20%) and state your assumptions.

cards.q: Explain three-point estimation with numbers.
cards.a: I take three values for a task: optimistic, most likely and pessimistic. The estimate is optimistic plus four times most likely plus pessimistic, divided by six. For example, 4 hours best case, 6 likely and 14 worst case gives (4 + 24 + 14) / 6 = 7 hours. The weighting pulls the estimate toward the likely value but accounts for risk.
cards.d:
Formula: E = (O + 4M + P) / 6. Standard deviation: SD = (P − O) / 6 → (14 − 4) / 6 ≈ 1.7, so say "7 hours, give or take about 2".

Practise with your own numbers until you can do it aloud.

cards.q: What is a WBS? Estimate testing a login page with it.
cards.a: WBS means breaking the work into small tasks that are easy to estimate, then adding them up. For a login page: analysing requirements half an hour, writing test cases two hours, test data half an hour, execution on three browsers and mobile three hours, bug reports and re-tests an hour and a half, regression one hour, reporting half an hour. That's nine hours; with a 15% buffer, about ten and a half.
cards.d:
Out loud, with WBS: clarify requirements and ask questions (0.5 h) → checklist/test cases: positive, negative, validation, UI, security basics, remember me, forgot password, lockout (2 h) → test data and accounts (0.5 h) → execution on 3 browsers + mobile (3 h) → bug reports and retests (1.5 h) → regression of related flows (1 h) → report (0.5 h). About 9 h + 15% buffer ≈ 10–11 h.

The interviewer cares about the method, not the number. Always include the things people forget: re-testing fixes, regression, environment setup and reporting.

cards.q: What factors affect a test estimate?
cards.a: The size and complexity of the feature; how clear and stable the requirements are; the number of platforms, browsers and devices; the team's experience and the tools available; how stable the test environment and builds are; how much test data is needed; and how many bugs we expect, because every bug adds reporting and re-testing time.
cards.d: Effort = analysis + design + setup + execution + re-tests + regression + reporting.

cards.q: How is work estimated in Agile? Story points, planning poker, velocity?
cards.a: In Agile, estimation is relative and done by the whole team. Story points measure the effort, complexity and risk of a story compared with other stories, usually on a Fibonacci scale. In planning poker everyone picks a card privately and reveals at once; the highest and lowest explain their reasoning and the team votes again. Velocity, the points finished per sprint, is then used to plan future sprints.
cards.d:
Story points often use the Fibonacci scale: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13.

This is also called "flexible estimation". Other relative scales: T-shirt sizes (S, M, L, XL). QA's part: make sure the estimate includes testing effort, not only coding.

cards.q: What risks are there in testing, and how do you handle them?
cards.a: Two types. Product risks are about the quality of the product: it might calculate wrongly, be slow, be insecure or be hard to use. Project risks are about the project's ability to deliver: unclear requirements, delays, people leaving, unstable environments or missing tools. Risk level is likelihood times impact, and risk-based testing means testing the highest product risks first and deepest. To handle them, I clarify requirements early, add buffers, prioritise by risk, keep a backup environment, and tell the PM about the risks in writing.
cards.d:
Main risks in testing: unclear or changing requirements, late builds, unstable environments, missing test data, lack of devices, tight deadlines, staff absence.

Mitigation: early clarification, buffers, risk-based prioritisation, backup environments or device farms, communicating risks to the PM in writing.

cards.q: When do you stop testing?
cards.a: Testing never proves there are no bugs, so we stop based on criteria, not perfection. Usually that means the exit criteria agreed in the test plan are met: planned tests run, no open critical bugs, an acceptable pass rate. Or the deadline arrives and the PM accepts the remaining risks, which I've reported. In continuous delivery, testing carries on with each new change.
cards.d:
Testing never "finishes"; we stop when the risk is acceptable: exit criteria are met (planned coverage reached, no open critical bugs, pass rate acceptable), or time/budget run out and the remaining risk is accepted by stakeholders.

Avoid "when the software works as intended": that moment never comes (principle #1).

cards.q: What is test reporting, and why is it needed?
cards.a: Test reporting is communicating the results and status of testing to stakeholders. It tells them what was tested, what was found and how good the product is, so they can decide whether to release, and it makes testing progress and risks visible to the team.
cards.d: Have three things ready: what a report is, the types, and the components.

cards.q: What types of test reports are there? Progress vs summary?
cards.a: Two main types. A test progress report, also called a status or interim report, is sent regularly during testing, daily, weekly or per sprint, and shows where we are and what blocks us. A test summary report, also called a final or completion report, is written at the end of a test cycle or release and gives the overall results and a release recommendation. Besides those, there are bug reports and automatic execution reports from tools like TestRail.
cards.d:
Progress (interim)Summary (final)
WhenDuring testing, regularlyAt the end of a cycle or release
FocusStatus, blockers, trendsResults, quality, recommendation
ReaderTeam, lead, PMPM, PO, client

cards.q: What goes into a test summary report? Show an example.
cards.a: It starts with the conclusion: the build, whether it's ready for release and why. Then scope: what was and wasn't tested. Then the numbers: test cases planned, run, passed, failed and blocked. Then defects by severity and status, with the open critical ones listed. Then risks and known issues with workarounds. For example: release 2.14 is ready with two known minor issues; 236 of 240 cases run, pass rate 97%; Apple Pay was not tested, and the PM accepted that risk.
cards.d:
• Project, release/build, environment, test period, who tested.
  • Scope: what was tested and what wasn't (and why).
  • Execution stats: planned / executed / passed / failed / blocked / skipped.
  • Defects: found, fixed, open, by severity/priority; list of open critical bugs.
  • Requirement coverage.
  • Deviations from the plan, risks, known issues and workarounds.
  • Conclusion and recommendation: ready / not ready for release.
Test Summary Report: Shop web, release 2.14, build 2.14.0-rc2
Period: 10–14 Nov, stage environment, Chrome / Safari / Firefox + iOS, Android

Conclusion: READY for release with 2 known minor issues.

Scope tested: checkout, promo codes, profile; full regression
Not tested:   Apple Pay (sandbox unavailable): risk accepted by PM

Test cases:  planned 240 | run 236 | passed 228 | failed 6 | blocked 2
Pass rate:   97%

Defects found: 14  (Critical 1, Major 4, Minor 7, Trivial 2)
Fixed and verified: 12
Open: 2 Minor (SHOP-512 label overlap on iPhone SE, SHOP-518 typo)

Risks: Apple Pay untested; monitor payments after release.

Managers read the conclusion first, so put it at the top.

cards.q: Which QA metrics do you know?
cards.a: I know several. Test execution progress is executed tests divided by planned tests. Pass rate is passed tests divided by executed tests. Defect density is the number of defects per size, for example per module or per story point. Defect leakage is bugs found in production divided by total bugs. Defect removal efficiency, or DRE, is bugs found before release divided by all bugs, before and after release, times 100 percent. I also know requirements coverage, reopened bug rate and average time to fix.
cards.d:
• Test execution progress = executed / planned.
  • Pass rate = passed / executed.
  • Defect density = defects / size (per module, per KLOC, per story point).
  • Defect leakage = bugs found in prod / total bugs.
  • DRE (defect removal efficiency) = bugs found before release / (before + after) × 100%.
  • Requirements coverage, reopened bug rate, average time to fix.

cards.q: Who reads test reports, and how do you adapt them?
cards.a: Different people read them, so I adapt the report to the reader. The PM and the PO want the summary, the risks and a go or no-go recommendation. Developers want the bug details. Clients want coverage and the quality status. So I lead with the conclusion and keep the details below for those who need them.
cards.d: PM and PO want the summary, risks and a go/no-go recommendation. Developers want bug details. Clients want coverage and quality status. Lead with the conclusion; keep details below for those who need them.

cards.q: How do you prioritise test cases?
cards.a: I use a risk-based approach: I rate each area by how likely it is to fail and how big the business impact would be, and I test the highest first. First comes smoke, to see that the app is testable at all. Then critical business flows like registration, login and payment. Then new and changed functionality and areas touched by fixes, then modules that had many bugs before, then frequently used features. Test cases also get priority labels, so regression can be cut quickly when time is short.
cards.d:
Risk-based testing: rate each area by probability of failure and business impact. Highest first:

  1. Smoke: the app is testable at all.
  2. Critical business flows: registration, login, payment, checkout.
  3. New and changed functionality, and areas touched by fixes.
  4. Historically bug-prone modules (defect clustering).
  5. Frequently used features, then everything else.

Test cases themselves get priority labels (High/Medium/Low, P1–P3) so regression can be cut quickly when time is short.

cards.q: What is risk-based testing?
cards.a: Risk-based testing is an approach where product risks decide which tests I choose, in what order I run them, and how deep I go. I identify the risks, assess the likelihood and impact of each one, and test high-risk areas first and more thoroughly. At the end I report the remaining risk. It is how I can defend the fact that we can't test everything.
cards.d: An approach where the selection, order and depth of tests are driven by product risks. Identify risks → assess likelihood and impact → test high-risk areas first and more thoroughly → report remaining risk. It's how you make "we can't test everything" defensible.

cards.q: What is MoSCoW?
cards.a: MoSCoW is a technique to prioritise requirements. It sorts them into four groups. Must have means the release fails without it. Should have means important, but not vital. Could have means nice to have. Won't have means we will not do it this time.
cards.d: A technique to prioritise requirements: Must have (release fails without it), Should have (important, not vital), Could have (nice to have), Won't have (this time).

cards.q: How do you distribute effort during testing?
cards.a: By risk. The areas with the highest business impact and the highest chance of failure get the most time and the earliest slot: critical flows, new and changed code, and modules with a history of bugs. Low-risk areas get lighter checks. Within a cycle I plan time for test design, execution, re-testing fixes and regression, not only the first run.
cards.d: Useful ideas to name: the Pareto principle (roughly 80% of defects come from 20% of modules) and shift-left (spend effort on requirements review early because it's cheapest there).

cards.q: What is defect management?
cards.a: The process of handling bugs from discovery to closure: logging them with clear reports, triaging them, which means confirming them and setting severity, priority and an owner, then fixing, re-testing and closing them. It also includes analysing the bugs afterwards: where they cluster and what the root causes are, to improve the process.
cards.d: Bug triage is a regular meeting of QA, a developer lead and the PM or PO to decide what gets fixed now, later or never.

cards.q: You have three urgent tasks from different people. What do you do?
cards.a: I don't silently pick one. I list the three tasks, estimate each one, and ask my lead or PM to set the order based on business priority. Then I tell the people who are waiting when they can expect their result. For my own planning I use the Eisenhower matrix, which sorts tasks by urgent and important.
cards.d: I don't silently pick one. I list them, estimate each, and ask my lead/PM to set the order based on business priority. Then I tell the people waiting when to expect their result. For my own planning I use the Eisenhower matrix (urgent/important).

cards.q: What tools does a QA engineer use, and what for?
cards.a: Jira for bugs and tasks, TestRail or Qase for test cases, Confluence for docs and Figma for designs. For technical work, Chrome DevTools and Charles to inspect traffic, Postman for APIs, and DBeaver for the database. For mobile, Android Studio and Xcode simulators.
cards.d:
Group them so it sounds organised:

PurposeTools
Tasks and bugs (tracking)Jira, YouTrack, Azure DevOps
Test cases (test management)TestRail, Zephyr, Qase
Docs and designsConfluence, Figma
APIPostman, Swagger
TrafficDevTools, Charles, Fiddler
DatabaseDBeaver, pgAdmin
MobileAndroid Studio + adb, Xcode simulators, TestFlight, BrowserStack
Cross-browserBrowserStack
Code and CIGit, Jenkins, GitHub Actions

An IDE matters mostly for automation.

Only claim what you have actually touched: say "I use" only for tools you've used; otherwise "I'm familiar with".

cards.q: What issue types are in Jira?
cards.a: The standard issue types in Jira are Epic, which is a big feature, Story, which is a user requirement, then Task, Bug and Sub-task. A project can also add its own custom types. Every issue moves through a workflow, which is a configurable set of statuses and transitions between them.
cards.d: Epic (big feature), Story (user requirement), Task, Bug, Sub-task. Projects can add custom types. Issues move through a configurable workflow (statuses + transitions).

cards.q: How do you work with issues in Jira: creating, linking, logging time?
cards.a: To create an issue I choose the project and issue type, then fill in the summary, description, priority, assignee, labels, components, the affected or fix version and the sprint, and attach files. I link issues to show relationships, for example a bug "is caused by" or "relates to" a story, "blocks" another task, or "duplicates" a bug. To log time I use Log work on the issue: time spent, the date and a comment; Jira then updates the remaining estimate.
cards.d:
• Issue types: Epic, Story, Task, Bug, Sub-task.
  • Link types: blocks / is blocked by, relates to, duplicates, clones, causes.
  • Time tracking fields: Original estimate, Time spent, Remaining.

cards.q: What are boards, filters and swimlanes in Jira?
cards.a: A board shows issues as cards in columns mapped to workflow statuses. A Scrum board works with sprints and a backlog; a Kanban board shows continuous flow. A filter is a saved search, written in JQL, that boards and dashboards are built on. Swimlanes are horizontal rows that group the cards on a board, for example by assignee, epic or priority.
cards.d:
project = SHOP AND issuetype = Bug AND status != Done
AND priority in (Highest, High) ORDER BY created DESC

Dashboards show gadgets (charts, filter results) built from filters.

cards.q: What is JQL? Give an example.
cards.a: JQL is Jira Query Language. I use it for advanced search and for filters in Jira. For example, to find the open, high-priority bugs assigned to me, I write: project equals SHOP, and issue type equals Bug, and status not in Closed or Done, and priority in Highest or High, and assignee equals current user, ordered by created date, newest first.
cards.d:
Jira Query Language for advanced search and filters:

project = SHOP AND issuetype = Bug
AND status not in (Closed, Done)
AND priority in (Highest, High)
AND assignee = currentUser()
ORDER BY created DESC

cards.q: What is a test management system for? How is TestRail organised?
cards.a: A test management system is for storing and organising test cases, planning test runs, recording results and reporting on coverage and progress. TestRail stores test cases in a project, grouped into suites and sections. To execute them I create a test run, pick the cases and set a result for each: Passed, Failed, Blocked, Retest or Untested. Several runs can be grouped into a test plan, and milestones track a release. Reports show run and milestone summaries, results over time, requirement coverage and defect summaries.
cards.d:
What a test management system (TMS) does: storing test cases and suites, organising them by feature, planning test runs per build, recording results (pass/fail/blocked), linking to Jira stories and bugs, and producing coverage and progress reports. Examples: TestRail, Zephyr, Xray, Qase.

Integration with Jira: from a failed test in TestRail you push a bug straight into Jira, link test cases to Jira stories as references, and see test results inside the Jira issue.

cards.q: What is CI/CD and how does QA fit in?
cards.a: CI is Continuous Integration: developers merge their code often, and each merge triggers an automatic build and tests. CD is Continuous Delivery or Deployment: every passing build can be released, or is released automatically. QA fits in by adding automated tests to the pipeline, testing the builds that come from it, and defining quality gates.
cards.d: Continuous Integration: developers merge often; each merge triggers an automatic build and tests. Continuous Delivery/Deployment: every passing build can be (or is automatically) released. QA adds automated tests to the pipeline, tests builds from it, and defines quality gates.

cards.q: What is test automation? What should and should not be automated?
cards.a: Test automation is using tools and scripts to run tests and compare results automatically. It saves time on repeated runs and gives fast feedback. Good candidates: regression and smoke tests, stable features, data-driven tests with many inputs, and API tests. Poor candidates: one-off checks, features that change every week, exploratory and usability testing, and anything that needs human judgement.
cards.d: Also know: CI = every merge triggers an automatic build and tests; Continuous Delivery = every passing build is ready to release with a manual approval; Continuous Deployment = it is released automatically.

cards.q: What is an operating system?
cards.a: An operating system is system software that manages the hardware resources of a computer: CPU, memory, storage and devices. It runs processes, provides a file system and security with users and permissions, and gives an interface, graphical or command line, for applications and users. Examples are Windows, macOS and Linux, and on mobile Android and iOS.
cards.d: System software that manages hardware resources (CPU, memory, storage, devices), runs processes, provides a file system, security (users, permissions) and an interface (GUI/CLI) for applications and users. Examples: Windows, macOS, Linux; mobile: Android, iOS.

cards.q: Windows vs Linux vs macOS for a tester?
cards.a: For a tester the key differences are practical. File names are case-sensitive on Linux, but not on Windows and not on macOS by default. Paths and line endings differ: Windows uses CRLF, Linux and macOS use LF. Installers differ too: exe and msi on Windows, deb and rpm on Linux, dmg and pkg on macOS. Logs are in Event Viewer on Windows, in /var/log on Linux and in the Console app on macOS. Fonts and rendering also differ, so I check the UI on each OS.
