WindowsLinuxmacOS
KernelNTLinuxXNU (Darwin, Unix)
File systemNTFSext4 and othersAPFS
PathsC:\Users\a/home/a/Users/a
Case-sensitive namesNoYesNo by default
Line endingsCRLFLFLF
Installers.exe .msi.deb .rpm, apt/dnf.dmg .pkg, App Store
LogsEvent Viewer/var/log, journalctlConsole app
Modifier keyCtrlCtrlCmd

Also: fonts and rendering differ, so check UI on each OS.

cards.q: Which Linux commands do you know, and what for?
cards.a: As a tester I mainly use Linux to investigate bugs on a test server. I connect with ssh, watch logs live with tail -f while reproducing the issue, search them with grep, check processes with ps and top, check disk space with df -h, and copy logs with scp to attach to bug reports.
cards.d:
ssh user@host                # connect
pwd  ls -la  cd              # move around
mkdir  touch  cp  mv  rm -r
cat  head
less app.log                 # scroll a big file
tail -f app.log              # follow a log live
grep "ERROR" app.log         # search
grep -i "error" app.log      # search in a file
find / -name "*.log"
chmod 755 file  chown user file  sudo
ps aux | grep java           # is the service running?
top                          # CPU and memory
kill -9 PID
df -h                        # is the disk full?
du -sh *  free -h
scp file user@host:/tmp
scp server:/logs/app.log .   # copy a file
curl  ping                   # requests, reachability
netstat / ss  man ls

cards.q: Explain Linux file permissions.
cards.a: Each file has permissions for the owner, the group and others. Each of them can have read, write and execute, with the values 4, 2 and 1. I add the values up: read, write and execute is 7, read and execute is 5, and read only is 4, so that file is set with chmod 754. Root is the superuser, and sudo runs a command as root.
cards.d: Each file has permissions for owner, group, others: read (r=4), write (w=2), execute (x=1). -rwxr-xr-- = owner rwx (7), group r-x (5), others r-- (4) → chmod 754. root is the superuser; sudo runs a command as root.

cards.q: Where do you find logs on each OS?
cards.a: On Windows I look in Event Viewer, under Windows Logs, Application or System. On Linux the logs are in the /var/log folder, and I can also use journalctl. On macOS I use the Console app or the Library/Logs folder in my home directory. There are also app-specific log files, and for web apps the server logs, which I reach through ssh, Kibana or Grafana.
cards.d: Windows: Event Viewer (Windows Logs → Application/System). Linux: /var/log/ (syslog, app folders), journalctl. macOS: Console app, ~/Library/Logs. Plus app-specific log files, and for web apps the server logs (via ssh, Kibana or Grafana).

cards.q: You have SSH access. How do you find an error in the server logs?
cards.a: I'd SSH into the server, open the app's log with tail -f, and reproduce the bug so I can see the error appear live. If I have an error code, I grep for it; if not, I search by timestamp, user ID or request ID, using grep -C to see the surrounding stack trace. Then I attach the relevant lines to the bug report.
cards.d:
grep -i "error" app.log
grep "2026-11-01 14:3" app.log
grep -C 5 "ERROR" app.log   # 5 lines of context

Logs usually live under /var/log/ or the app's own folder; ask the developers.

cards.q: Useful Windows commands?
cards.a: For the network I use ipconfig to see my IP, and ipconfig /flushdns to flush DNS, plus ping, tracert, nslookup and netstat -ano. For processes I use tasklist and taskkill with a process ID. systeminfo shows system information, and dir and cd are for folders. I also know the hosts file in Windows\System32\drivers\etc: it is handy to point a domain at a test server.
cards.d: ipconfig (IP; /flushdns), ping, tracert, nslookup, netstat -ano, tasklist, taskkill /PID, systeminfo, dir, cd. Hosts file: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts (on Linux/macOS: /etc/hosts), handy to point a domain at a test server.

cards.q: What is the Windows Registry?
cards.a: A hierarchical database where Windows and installed programs store their settings. You open it with regedit. It's organised into root keys such as HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE for settings of the whole computer and HKEY_CURRENT_USER for the logged-in user. A tester uses it to check that an installer writes its keys and removes them on uninstall, or to change an app's settings for a test.
cards.d: The five root keys: HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT, HKEY_CURRENT_USER, HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, HKEY_USERS, HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG. Basic cmd commands to know: dir, cd, ipconfig, ping, tracert, netstat, tasklist, taskkill.

cards.q: Process vs thread?
cards.a: A process is a running program with its own memory space. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process, and the threads of one process share its memory. For example, a browser uses multiple processes, so the tabs are isolated from each other, and many threads.
cards.d: A process is a running program with its own memory space. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process; threads of one process share its memory. A browser uses multiple processes (tabs isolated) and many threads.

cards.q: What is a version control system, and why does QA need it?
cards.a: A version control system, like Git, tracks every change to the code, keeps the history, and lets people work in parallel on branches and merge them. As a tester I use it to check out and test specific branches, look at what changed in a release to plan regression, and find when a bug was introduced. If I write autotests, they live in Git too.
cards.d:
A version control system records changes to files over time so you can see history, compare versions, work in parallel on branches and revert.

QA uses it to: check out and run a specific branch/build, store and review autotest code, see what changed in a release to scope regression, and find the commit that introduced a bug (git bisect).

Creating and merging branches is mostly what developers and automation testers do. For manual QA, emphasise reading changes and testing branches.

cards.q: What types of version control systems are there?
cards.a: Three types. Local systems keep versions on one computer only. Centralized systems, like SVN and CVS, have one central server holding the history; everyone needs a connection to it, and it's a single point of failure. Distributed systems, like Git and Mercurial, give every developer a full copy of the repository with its history, so you can work offline and branching is cheap.
cards.d:
Centralized (SVN)Distributed (Git)
HistoryOn the server onlyFull copy on every machine
Offline workNo commitsCommit locally, push later
Server downWork stopsWork continues
BranchingHeavyFast and cheap

cards.q: Git vs GitHub?
cards.a: Git is the version control tool itself. GitHub is a hosting service for Git repositories, and GitLab and Bitbucket are similar services. On top of Git it adds collaboration features: pull requests, code review, issues, and CI with GitHub Actions. So Git tracks the changes, and GitHub is where the team keeps the repository and reviews the code.
cards.d: Git is the version control tool itself. GitHub (also GitLab, Bitbucket) is a hosting service for Git repositories with collaboration features: pull requests, code review, issues, CI (Actions).

cards.q: Describe the basic Git workflow and commands.
cards.a: I clone the repository, create a branch, change files, stage them with git add, commit, and push the branch, then open a pull request to merge it. To get others' changes I pull. After review the branch is merged into main. Other commands I use are git status, git log, git diff, git stash and git merge.
cards.d:
git clone <url>
git switch -c feature/login-tests   # new branch
# edit files
git status
git add .                            # stage
git commit -m "Add login tests"      # local commit
git push -u origin feature/login-tests
# open a Pull/Merge Request → review → merge into main
git pull          # fetch + merge
git log / git diff / git stash / git merge

cards.q: git fetch vs git pull?
cards.a: git fetch downloads new commits from the remote, but it doesn't change my working branch. git pull is fetch plus merge: it downloads the new commits and then merges them, or rebases, into my current branch. So with fetch I only get the new commits, and with pull my branch is updated right away.
cards.d: fetch downloads new commits from the remote but doesn't change your working branch. pull = fetch + merge (or rebase) into your current branch.

cards.q: merge vs rebase?
cards.a: Merge joins two branches with a merge commit, and the history is preserved as it happened. Rebase replays my commits on top of another branch, so the history becomes linear, but the commits are rewritten. Because of that, I don't rebase shared or public branches.
cards.d: Merge joins two branches with a merge commit; history is preserved as it happened. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch; history becomes linear but commits are rewritten. Don't rebase shared/public branches.

cards.q: revert vs reset?
cards.a: git revert creates a new commit that undoes a previous one, so it is safe for shared history. git reset moves the branch pointer back: soft keeps the changes staged, mixed keeps them unstaged, and hard discards them. Reset rewrites history, so I use it only locally.
cards.d: git revert <commit> creates a new commit that undoes a previous one; safe for shared history. git reset moves the branch pointer back (soft keeps changes staged, mixed keeps them unstaged, hard discards them); rewrites history, use locally only.

cards.q: What is a merge conflict?
cards.a: A merge conflict happens when two branches change the same lines of a file differently, so Git can't merge them automatically. Someone has to open the file, choose or combine the versions between the conflict markers, and commit the result.
cards.d:
A conflict also happens when one branch deleted a file the other edited. The conflict markers are <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>; after you choose or combine the versions, you add and commit.

<<<<<<< HEAD
price = 100
=======
price = 120
>>>>>>> feature-sale

cards.q: What branching strategies do you know? What is Git Flow?
cards.a: I know three branching strategies: Git Flow, GitHub Flow and trunk-based development. Git Flow is a branching model: main holds production code, develop holds the next release, features are built in feature branches off develop, releases are stabilised in release branches, and urgent production fixes go through hotfix branches. GitHub Flow is simpler: main plus short feature branches merged through pull requests. In trunk-based development everyone commits small changes to main often, with feature flags.
cards.d:
• Git Flow: main (production), develop, feature/*, release/*, hotfix/*.
  • GitHub Flow: main + short feature branches merged via PR.
  • Trunk-based: everyone commits small changes to main often, with feature flags.

QA tests feature branches on dev/stage environments and release branches before production.

cards.q: What are git stash and cherry-pick?
cards.a: git stash temporarily shelves my uncommitted changes so I can switch branches, and git stash pop brings them back. git cherry-pick with a commit hash copies one specific commit onto the current branch. A typical example is taking a hotfix commit into a release branch.
cards.d: stash temporarily shelves uncommitted changes so you can switch branches; stash pop brings them back. cherry-pick <hash> copies one specific commit onto the current branch (e.g. a hotfix into a release branch).

cards.q: What is a virtual machine, and why would a tester use one?
cards.a: A virtual machine is a virtual computer running its own OS on top of my real machine, through a hypervisor like VirtualBox or VMware. Testers use VMs to test on other operating systems and browser versions, and above all for snapshots: you can roll back to a clean state after installing or breaking things.
cards.d:
A VM is a software emulation of a computer that runs its own (guest) OS on top of a physical (host) machine, managed by a hypervisor. Type 1 runs on bare metal (VMware ESXi, Hyper-V); type 2 runs inside a host OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Parallels).

  • Testers also use VMs to keep isolated clean environments.
  • Snapshots are ideal for installation and upgrade testing; VMs are also useful for compatibility testing.
  • macOS is licensed only for Apple hardware: for Mac testing use a real Mac or BrowserStack.

cards.q: VM vs Docker container?
cards.a: A VM virtualises hardware and runs a full OS with its own kernel, so it is heavier, takes minutes to start, and gives strong isolation. A container shares the kernel of the host OS and packages only the app and its dependencies, so it is lightweight and starts in seconds. Teams use Docker to spin up identical test environments quickly.
cards.d: A VM virtualises hardware and runs a full OS with its own kernel: heavier, minutes to start, strong isolation. A container shares the host OS kernel and packages only the app and its dependencies: lightweight, starts in seconds. Teams use Docker to spin up identical test environments quickly.

cards.q: What is RDP?
cards.a: RDP is Microsoft's Remote Desktop Protocol, for connecting to and controlling a remote Windows machine's desktop over the network, on port 3389 by default. Testers use it to work on remote test machines, like a Windows box with specific software or a machine inside a client's network.
cards.d: Alternatives: VNC, TeamViewer, AnyDesk, Chrome Remote Desktop; SSH gives a Linux command line rather than a desktop.

cards.q: What is remote administration? Types and programs?
cards.a: Remote administration is controlling a computer or server from another location over the network. There are two main types. Graphical remote desktop gives you the screen, mouse and keyboard: RDP for Windows, VNC, TeamViewer, AnyDesk and Chrome Remote Desktop. Command-line access gives you a terminal: SSH for Linux and macOS servers. Testers use these to work on remote test machines and to read logs on servers.
cards.d: Ports worth knowing: RDP 3389, SSH 22, VNC 5900. Telnet is the old, unencrypted predecessor of SSH.

cards.q: What is a VPN, and when does a tester need one?
cards.a: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between my device and another network, so my traffic appears to come from there. As a tester I mostly use it to reach internal or client test environments that aren't public. I'd also use it to check geo-dependent behaviour, like prices or content in other countries.
cards.d:
VPN stands for Virtual Private Network; the tunnel goes between your device and a network/server.

Geo-dependent behaviour to test: localisation, prices, content restrictions by country.

A VPN isn't a single protocol; it runs over OpenVPN, WireGuard or IPsec/IKEv2. Changing your IP is a side effect, not the purpose.

cards.q: What is a proxy server?
cards.a: A proxy server is an intermediary between the client and the server that forwards requests. It is used for caching, filtering, anonymity and load balancing; a reverse proxy like nginx is an example. In testing I use a debugging proxy such as Charles or Fiddler to inspect and modify traffic.
cards.d: An intermediary between client and server that forwards requests. Used for caching, filtering, anonymity, load balancing (reverse proxy, e.g. nginx), and in testing to inspect and modify traffic (Charles, Fiddler are debugging proxies).

cards.q: What is a CMS, and what would you test in one?
cards.a: A CMS, like WordPress, lets non-technical people manage website content through an admin panel. I'd test roles and permissions, the publishing workflow including scheduling, that editor content renders the same on the live site, media uploads, that changes really appear despite caching, and that plugin updates don't break anything.
cards.d:
A Content Management System lets non-developers create, edit and publish website content through an admin UI. Examples: WordPress, Drupal, Joomla; headless: Strapi, Contentful; e-commerce: Shopify, Magento.

Test: roles and permissions (editor vs admin), content workflow (draft → review → publish → unpublish), WYSIWYG editor output, media upload (formats, sizes), SEO fields and URLs, scheduling, versioning/rollback, plugins and themes compatibility after updates, caching (does the change show on the site?), and that published content renders correctly on the front end.

Reason from the name when unsure: "it manages content, so I'd test creating, editing and publishing content, and who's allowed to do it."

cards.q: What are IP address, DNS, port, localhost?
cards.a: An IP address is the network address of a device, in IPv4 or IPv6 format. DNS translates domain names into IP addresses. A port is a number that identifies a service on a host: for example 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS and 22 for SSH. Localhost is my own machine, with the address 127.0.0.1.
cards.d: IP: network address of a device (IPv4 192.168.0.10, IPv6). DNS: translates domain names to IPs. Port: number identifying a service on a host (80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 22 SSH, 3389 RDP, 5432 PostgreSQL, 3306 MySQL). localhost = 127.0.0.1, your own machine.

cards.q: What is client-server architecture? Who is the client and who is the server?
cards.a: It's a model where the work is split between two roles. The client sends requests and shows results to the user: a browser, a mobile app or a desktop app. The server receives requests, runs the business logic, works with the database and sends back responses. They talk over a network using a protocol, usually HTTP. One server serves many clients.
cards.d:
Example to say: "When I open a shop site, my browser is the client; it sends GET /products; the shop's server queries its database and returns the product list."

For a tester this split matters because a bug is either on the client side (wrong request, wrong display) or the server side (wrong response).

cards.q: What types of client-server architecture are there?
cards.a: By the number of tiers. In a two-tier architecture the client talks directly to the server that holds the data. In a three-tier architecture there are three layers: the presentation layer, which is the client; the application server with the business logic; and the database server. Multi-tier adds more layers, like load balancers, caches and separate services. Most web applications are three-tier or multi-tier.
cards.d:
• Thin client: the logic runs on the server; the client only displays (a browser).
  • Thick client: much of the processing runs on the user's machine (a desktop app, a game).
  • One-tier: everything on one machine. Peer-to-peer is the alternative model, where each node is both client and server.

cards.q: What is a firewall?
cards.a: A firewall is a security system that filters network traffic going in and out, based on rules: which IP addresses, ports and protocols are allowed. It can be hardware or software. A web application firewall, or WAF, protects a web app specifically by blocking suspicious requests, like injection attempts.
cards.d: Why a tester meets it: a test environment behind a firewall is reachable only through VPN; a blocked port explains a "cannot connect" problem; a WAF may block your negative security tests.

cards.q: What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?
cards.a: The browser resolves the domain to an IP through DNS, opens a TCP connection, and for HTTPS does a TLS handshake to verify the certificate. Then it sends an HTTP request; the server processes it, maybe queries the database, and returns a response with a status code and HTML. Finally the browser parses the HTML, loads the CSS, JS and images, and renders the page.
cards.d:
1. Browser parses the URL; checks its cache.
  2. DNS lookup: browser cache → OS cache/hosts → resolver → root → TLD → authoritative server → IP address.
  3. TCP connection (3-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK).
  4. TLS handshake for HTTPS: certificate check, keys agreed.
  5. Browser sends the HTTP request (GET /, headers, cookies).
  6. Server (web server → app → DB) processes it and returns a response (status code, headers, HTML).
  7. Browser parses HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM, requests images/CSS/JS, runs JS, builds the render tree, layout, paint.

Each step breaks differently: DNS errors, certificate warnings, 500s, slow responses, broken CSS.

Memory hook: find the address → connect → secure → ask → server works → answer → draw.

cards.q: Website vs web application? SPA vs MPA?
cards.a: A website is mostly informational, while a web application is interactive, like Gmail or Jira. In a multi-page application, an MPA, each navigation loads a new HTML page from the server. In a single-page application, an SPA, one page loads, and then JavaScript updates the content through API calls without full reloads; React, Angular and Vue work this way. When I test an SPA, I check the browser back and forward buttons, deep links, and refresh on inner routes.
cards.d: A website is mostly informational; a web app is interactive (Gmail, Jira). MPA: each navigation loads a new HTML page from the server. SPA: one page loads, then JS updates content via API calls without full reloads (React, Angular, Vue). In SPAs check browser back/forward, deep links and refresh on inner routes.

cards.q: What do you check when testing a web application?
cards.a: First I check functionality: links, forms, validation, navigation, search, login and the business flows. Then the UI: it matches the design, and states like hover, disabled and error look right. Next, compatibility with different browsers and operating systems, and responsive layout at breakpoints and on mobile. I also check usability and accessibility, like keyboard navigation and contrast; performance, such as load time and behaviour on a slow network; and basic security: HTTPS, access control by URL, session expiry, and XSS or SQL injection in inputs. Finally cookies, sessions, cache and localisation.
cards.d:
• Functional: links, forms, validation, navigation, search, auth, business flows.
  • UI: matches design (Figma), fonts, colours, alignment, states (hover, disabled, error).
  • Compatibility: browsers and versions, OSes.
  • Responsive: breakpoints, mobile, orientation.
  • Usability and accessibility (keyboard navigation, alt texts, contrast, screen readers, WCAG).
  • Performance: load time, Lighthouse, behaviour on slow network.
  • Security basics: HTTPS, access control by URL, session expiry, XSS/SQL injection in inputs.
  • Cookies, sessions, cache; localisation; SEO basics (titles, meta, 404 page).

cards.q: How would you test a registration form?
cards.a: I'd check validation first: required fields, field lengths with boundary values, email and phone formats, spaces and special characters, and an already-registered email, plus clear error messages. Then behaviour: double-clicking submit, back and refresh, slow network, and that the confirmation email arrives. I'd verify the server also validates, by removing restrictions in DevTools. Finally the UI, across browsers and on mobile.
cards.d:
1. Fields: required fields; valid/invalid formats (email, phone); EP + BVA on lengths and numbers; leading/trailing spaces; special characters, emoji, Cyrillic; copy-paste; existing email; password masking; error messages (text, position, when they appear).
  2. Behaviour: tab order and Enter to submit; double-click submit (no duplicates); back button and refresh after submit; behaviour on slow network; confirmation email.
  3. Security: server-side validation (remove the maxlength/required attribute in DevTools and submit); HTML/script and SQL in inputs do nothing.
  4. Look: design, browsers, mobile, keyboard-only use.

"What inputs work" is vague; name the techniques.

cards.q: Cookies vs localStorage vs sessionStorage?
cards.a: Both store data in the browser. Cookies are small, about 4 KB, can expire, and are sent to the server with every request, which is why they hold session IDs for login. localStorage holds more, about 5 MB, stays until cleared, and is never sent to the server, so it's for things like settings. sessionStorage is like localStorage but is cleared when the tab closes.
cards.d:
CookieslocalStoragesessionStorage
Size~4 KB~5–10 MB~5 MB
Sent to serverYes, with every requestNoNo
LifetimeUntil Expires/Max-Age, or sessionUntil clearedUntil tab closes
AccessServer + JS (unless HttpOnly)JSJS, per tab

Cookie attributes: Domain, Path, Expires, Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite.

HttpOnly cookies can't be read by JavaScript. Test in DevTools → Application: delete the session cookie and reload (logged out?), clear localStorage (cart empty?).

cards.q: What is a session? How does the site remember you are logged in?
cards.a: HTTP is stateless, so the server does not remember me between requests. After I log in, the server creates a session and sends its ID to the browser in a cookie. The browser sends that cookie with every request, and this is how the site knows I am logged in. Another way is a token, often a JWT: the client stores it and sends it in the Authorization header. As a tester I check that logout and timeout end the session, and that deleting the cookie logs me out.
cards.d: HTTP is stateless, so after login the server creates a session and sends its ID in a cookie (Set-Cookie: sessionid=…); the browser sends it with every request. Alternatively a token (often a JWT) is stored by the client and sent in the Authorization: Bearer header. Test: logout invalidates it, session timeout, behaviour in two tabs/devices, deleting the cookie logs you out.

cards.q: What is cache, and how do you deal with it when testing?
cards.a: Cache is a stored copy of resources like images, styles and scripts, kept so pages load faster next time. The problem for testing is that an old cached file can hide a fix. So I do a hard reload with Ctrl+Shift+R, tick "Disable cache" in the DevTools Network tab, use an incognito window, or clear site data. I also check that users get the new version after a release.
cards.d:
Stored copies of resources (browser cache, CDN, server cache) to load faster. Stale cache hides fixes, so: hard reload (Ctrl+Shift+R / Cmd+Shift+R), DevTools → Network → "Disable cache", incognito window, or clear site data in Application tab.

Cache vs cookies: cache stores files to speed up loading; cookies store small data about the user and are sent to the server.

cards.q: Responsive vs adaptive design?
cards.a: Responsive design is one fluid layout that continuously adjusts to any screen width, using flexible grids, percent units and media queries. Adaptive design has several fixed layouts, and one of them is chosen for each breakpoint or device. When I test, I check at the breakpoints and around them, in both orientations, on real devices and in DevTools device mode.
cards.d: Responsive: one fluid layout that continuously adjusts to any width (flexible grids, % units, media queries). Adaptive: several fixed layouts, one chosen per breakpoint/device. Test at and around breakpoints, in both orientations, with real devices plus DevTools device mode.

cards.q: What types of web vulnerabilities do you know?
cards.a: Injection, such as SQL injection, where input is executed as a command. Cross-site scripting, XSS, where a script typed into a field runs in another user's browser. Broken access control, for example opening another user's data by changing an ID in the URL. Broken authentication, like weak passwords or sessions that don't expire. CSRF, where a user's browser is tricked into sending a request. And security misconfiguration, like default passwords or open admin pages.
cards.d: The reference list is the OWASP Top 10. Simple manual checks: type <script>alert(1)</script> into text fields; change IDs in URLs; open admin URLs as a normal user; check logout really ends the session; check passwords aren't in URLs.

cards.q: What is SQL injection? Have you used injections in practice?
cards.a: SQL injection is when user input is inserted into a database query without protection, so an attacker can change the query. For example, typing ' OR '1'='1 into a login field can make the condition always true and log the attacker in. The protection is parameterised queries and input validation. In practice I've tried basic injections like that in login and search fields on test environments, to check the application rejects them, never on a production system without permission.
cards.d:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE login = 'INPUT' AND password = '...'
-- input:  ' OR '1'='1' --
SELECT * FROM users WHERE login = '' OR '1'='1' --' AND password = '...'

If you haven't tried it, do it once on a practice site such as the login of an intentionally vulnerable demo app, so your answer is true.

cards.q: Which basic security checks can a manual tester do?
cards.a: I check that HTTPS is used everywhere. I change an ID in the URL to try to open another user's pages or data, which is called IDOR, and I open admin URLs as a normal user. I check that the session ends after logout and after timeout, and that passwords are masked and never appear in URLs or logs. I enter a script tag with an alert in input fields to check it isn't executed, which is XSS, and a simple SQL injection string to check it doesn't break queries. I also check brute-force protection on login. My reference is the OWASP Top 10.
cards.d: HTTPS everywhere; access pages/API of another user by changing an ID in the URL (IDOR); open admin URLs as a normal user; session ends after logout and timeout; passwords masked and not in URLs/logs; input of <script>alert(1)</script> isn't executed (XSS); ' OR 1=1 -- doesn't break queries (SQL injection); brute-force protection on login. Reference: OWASP Top 10.

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.q: What is a protocol?
cards.a: A protocol is a set of rules for how devices exchange data over a network: the format of the messages, their order, and how errors are handled. Examples: HTTP and HTTPS for the web, TCP and UDP for transport, IP for addressing, FTP for files, SMTP for sending email, DNS for resolving names, and SSH for secure remote access.
cards.d: HTTP specifically: an application-layer, stateless, request-response protocol between client and server.

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.q: Describe the OSI model.
cards.a: The OSI model describes network communication in seven layers. From the bottom: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. IP works at the network layer, TCP and UDP at the transport layer, and HTTP at the application layer.
cards.d:
7 layers, bottom to top: 1 Physical (cables, signals), 2 Data link (Ethernet, MAC, switches), 3 Network (IP, routing), 4 Transport (TCP, UDP, ports), 5 Session, 6 Presentation (encoding, encryption), 7 Application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS). The practical TCP/IP model has 4: Link, Internet, Transport, Application.

TCP is reliable and ordered (web, email); UDP is fast with no delivery guarantee (calls, streaming, games).

Mnemonic, bottom to top: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.q: TCP vs UDP?
cards.a: TCP is connection-oriented: it starts with a handshake, and it gives reliable, ordered delivery, because lost data is sent again. That makes it slower. It's used for web, email and file transfer. UDP is connectionless: it gives no guarantee of delivery or order, but it's fast and has low overhead. It's used for video and voice calls, streaming, online games and DNS.
cards.d: TCP: connection-oriented (handshake), reliable, ordered delivery with retransmission; slower. Used for web, email, file transfer. UDP: connectionless, no delivery or order guarantee, fast, low overhead. Used for video/voice calls, streaming, online games, DNS.

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.q: What other protocols do you know?
cards.a: Besides HTTP, I know FTP and SFTP for transferring files, SMTP for sending mail, and IMAP and POP3 for receiving mail. I also know DNS, SSH and DHCP. WebSocket is a persistent two-way connection, with addresses that start with ws or wss, and it's used for chats and live updates. And there's MQTT for IoT devices, and gRPC.
cards.d: FTP/SFTP (files), SMTP (send mail), IMAP/POP3 (receive mail), DNS, SSH, DHCP, WebSocket (persistent two-way connection, ws:///wss://, for chats and live updates), MQTT (IoT), gRPC.

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.q: What is HTTP? HTTP vs HTTPS?
cards.a: HTTP is the HyperText Transfer Protocol: a stateless, client-server request and response protocol for the web. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. The traffic is encrypted so nobody in between can read or change it, and the server proves its identity with a certificate the browser checks. HTTP uses port 80, HTTPS port 443. As a tester I check for certificate errors and mixed content, and I install a proxy certificate when I need to inspect HTTPS traffic in Charles.
cards.d:
HTTP is an application-layer protocol.

Three guarantees of HTTPS: encryption, integrity, authentication (the certificate, shown as the padlock).

Versions: HTTP/1.1 (text), HTTP/2 (binary, multiplexing), HTTP/3 (over QUIC/UDP).

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.q: What are the parts of a URL?
cards.a: A URL starts with the scheme, for example https. Then comes the host, which is the subdomain plus the domain, like shop.example.com. After the host there can be a port, like 443. Then the path, for example /catalog/items. After the question mark come the query parameters, like id=42 and sort=asc. At the end, after the hash sign, is the fragment, which is not sent to the server.
cards.d: https://user@shop.example.com:443/catalog/items?id=42&sort=asc#reviews → scheme https, host (subdomain + domain) shop.example.com, port 443, path /catalog/items, query parameters id=42&sort=asc, fragment #reviews (not sent to the server).

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.q: What does an HTTP request and response consist of?
cards.a: A request has a first line with the method, the path and the HTTP version, for example POST /api/users. Then come the headers, like Host, Content-Type and Authorization, then an empty line, and then the body, for example JSON. A response has a first line with the version, the status code and the reason, like 201 Created. Then again headers, like Content-Type and Location, an empty line, and the body.
cards.d:
POST /api/users HTTP/1.1          ← method, path, version
Host: example.com                  ← headers
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
                                   ← empty line
{"name":"Ann","job":"QA"}          ← body

HTTP/1.1 201 Created               ← version, status code, reason
Content-Type: application/json
Location: /api/users/42

{"id":42,"name":"Ann","job":"QA"}

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.q: Which HTTP methods do you know?
cards.a: GET reads a resource, POST creates one, PUT replaces a resource completely, PATCH updates part of it, and DELETE removes it. HEAD returns only headers and OPTIONS returns the allowed methods. PUT sends the whole object and overwrites it; PATCH sends only the fields to change.
cards.d:
MethodPurposeIdempotentSafe
GETRead a resourceYesYes
POSTCreate / submit dataNoNo
PUTReplace whole resourceYesNo
PATCHPartial updateNot guaranteedNo
DELETEDeleteYesNo
HEADLike GET, headers onlyYesYes
OPTIONSAllowed methods; CORS preflightYesYes

Idempotent: repeating the request leaves the server in the same state. Safe: doesn't change server state.

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.q: GET vs POST?
cards.a: GET reads data and POST sends data, for example to create something. GET puts its parameters in the URL, so it can be cached and bookmarked, but it has length limits and shows up in logs, so no passwords. POST sends data in the request body. GET should be safe to repeat; repeating a POST might, for example, create a duplicate order.
cards.d:
Both requests send and receive; the difference is purpose, not direction.

GETPOST
PurposeReadSend or create
ParametersIn the URL query stringIn the body
RepeatableYes (safe and idempotent)May duplicate (not safe, not idempotent)
Cache, bookmark, history, server logsYesNormally not
SizeLimited by URL lengthBody can be large (files)

Neither is "secure" by itself: over HTTPS both are encrypted, but GET parameters still leak into history and logs, so never put passwords or tokens in a GET URL.

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.q: PUT vs PATCH vs POST?
cards.a: POST creates a new resource: the server assigns the ID, and repeating the request creates duplicates. PUT replaces a resource completely: it sends the whole object and overwrites it, so missing fields are cleared. PATCH updates part of it: it sends only the fields to change. For example, POST /users creates a user, PUT /users/42 replaces user 42 entirely, and PATCH /users/42 changes only the fields I send. PUT is idempotent; POST is not.
cards.d:
POST /users creates a new user (server assigns the ID; repeating creates duplicates). PUT /users/42 replaces user 42 entirely with the body sent (missing fields are cleared). PATCH /users/42 changes only the fields sent.

The other main methods: GET reads a resource and DELETE removes it. HEAD returns only headers and OPTIONS returns the allowed methods.

Idempotent (repeating gives the same result): GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS. Not idempotent: POST.

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.q: Name the status code classes and common codes.
cards.a: 1xx is information, 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx a client error (your request is wrong), 5xx a server error. Common ones: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content; 301 and 302 redirects, 304 Not Modified; 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests; 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout.
cards.d:
ClassCodes
1xx Informational100 Continue, 101 Switching Protocols (WebSocket)
2xx Success200 OK, 201 Created, 202 Accepted, 204 No Content
3xx Redirection301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified, 307 Temporary Redirect, 308 Permanent Redirect
4xx Client error400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 408 Request Timeout, 409 Conflict, 413 Payload Too Large, 415 Unsupported Media Type, 422 Unprocessable Content, 429 Too Many Requests
5xx Server error500 Internal Server Error, 501 Not Implemented, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout

503 = server up but temporarily unable to handle requests (overload or maintenance). A 5xx means the problem is on the server side, so a valid request that returns 5xx is worth reporting.

Memory hooks: 2xx "here you go", 3xx "go over there", 4xx "you messed up", 5xx "we messed up".

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.a: 401 means the server doesn't know who you are: no login or an expired token, so logging in fixes it. 403 means it knows who you are, but you're not allowed. For example, a regular user opening an admin page. Logging in again won't help there.
cards.d: 401 Unauthorized really means unauthenticated: the server doesn't know who you are (no token, expired or invalid credentials). Log in and retry. 403 Forbidden: the server knows who you are, but you don't have rights to this resource.

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.a: All four are server errors. 500 is an unhandled error in the application itself. 502 Bad Gateway means a gateway or proxy, like nginx or a load balancer, got an invalid response from the upstream server, for example because the app crashed. 503 Service Unavailable means the server temporarily can't handle requests, because of overload or maintenance. 504 Gateway Timeout means the proxy didn't get a response from the upstream server in time.
cards.d: 500: an unhandled error in the application itself. 502 Bad Gateway: a gateway/proxy (nginx, load balancer) got an invalid response from the upstream server (e.g. app crashed). 503 Service Unavailable: server temporarily can't handle requests (overload, maintenance). 504 Gateway Timeout: the proxy didn't get a response from upstream in time.

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.a: 301 is a permanent move: browsers and search engines remember the new URL. 302 is temporary: the client keeps using the old URL. 307 and 308 are the temporary and permanent versions that guarantee the method and body are kept, so a POST stays a POST. In all of them the new location is in the Location header.
cards.d: 301: permanent move: browsers and search engines remember the new URL. 302: temporary: keep using the old URL. 307/308 are the temporary/permanent versions that guarantee the method and body are kept (a POST stays a POST). New location is in the Location header. 304 Not Modified: use your cached copy.

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.q: Status code drill: which code in each case?
cards.a: Created: 201. Requesting something that doesn't exist: 404. No token: 401. A normal user on an admin endpoint: 403. Invalid JSON: 400. Server crash: 500. Email already exists: 409. Too many requests: 429.
cards.d:
The five groups first, then these by heart:

GroupMeaningKnow these
1xxInformational100, 101
2xxSuccess200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
3xxRedirection301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified
4xxClient error400, 401, 403, 404, 405, 409, 429
5xxServer error500, 502, 503, 504

More cases: successful delete with no body → 204; wrong method → 405; old URL moved → 301; server down for maintenance → 503; proxy got no answer in time → 504.

cards.t: Protocols, HTTP methods and status codes
cards.q: Which HTTP headers do you know?
cards.a: For requests I know Host, User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Language, Content-Type, Content-Length, Authorization, Cookie, Origin, Referer and Cache-Control. For responses: Content-Type, Set-Cookie, Location, Cache-Control, ETag, Access-Control-Allow-Origin, which is for CORS, and Server. For example, Content-Type tells the format of the body, Authorization carries the token, and Set-Cookie tells the browser to save a cookie.
cards.d: Request: Host, User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Language, Content-Type, Content-Length, Authorization, Cookie, Origin, Referer, Cache-Control. Response: Content-Type, Set-Cookie, Location, Cache-Control, ETag, Access-Control-Allow-Origin (CORS), Server.

cards.q: What is an API?
cards.a: An API is a contract that lets programs talk to each other. It defines which endpoints exist, what requests to send and what responses come back. For example, a mobile app calls GET /api/orders and gets the user's orders as JSON. The most common style is REST; others are SOAP and GraphQL.
cards.d:
Application Programming Interface: a defined set of rules (endpoints, methods, request/response formats) through which one program uses another's functionality or data. Types: REST, SOAP, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSocket.

Example: a mobile app's frontend asks the backend GET /api/orders and gets JSON back.

Everyday example: a weather app doesn't measure the weather; it calls a weather service's API.

cards.q: What is REST, and what are its principles?
cards.a: REST is an architectural style for APIs over HTTP. Its principles: client and server are separate; the server is stateless, so each request carries everything needed; responses can be cached; there's a uniform interface where each resource has its own URL and is handled with the standard HTTP methods; and the system can be layered, with proxies or gateways in between.
cards.d:
REST stands for REpresentational State Transfer. It is an architectural style, not a protocol. Constraints:

  • Client-server separation
  • Stateless: each request has all the info needed; server keeps no client session
  • Cacheable responses
  • Uniform interface: resources identified by URIs (/users/42), manipulated with HTTP methods, self-descriptive messages
  • Layered system (proxies, gateways)
  • Code on demand (optional)

Good REST: nouns in URLs (GET /users/42/orders, not /getOrders), correct methods and correct status codes.

cards.q: What does a SOAP message consist of? What is WSDL?
cards.a: A SOAP message is an XML document with an Envelope as the root element. Inside it there's an optional Header, for things like authentication, and a Body with the actual request or response data. Errors are returned in a Fault element inside the Body. WSDL is an XML file that describes the web service: which operations it has, the format of their messages, and the address to call.
cards.d:
<soap:Envelope>
  <soap:Header>…</soap:Header>
  <soap:Body>
    <GetUser><Id>42</Id></GetUser>
  </soap:Body>
</soap:Envelope>

cards.q: Five differences between REST and SOAP, and when to choose each.
cards.a: One: REST is an architectural style, SOAP is a protocol. Two: REST usually uses JSON, SOAP only XML. Three: REST uses many URLs and the HTTP methods; SOAP usually sends POST to one endpoint. Four: SOAP requires a WSDL contract; REST's OpenAPI description is optional. Five: REST is lighter and faster; SOAP is heavier but has built-in standards for security and transactions. I'd choose REST for web and mobile apps, and SOAP for banking or legacy enterprise integrations that need strict contracts.
cards.d:
RESTSOAP
NatureArchitectural styleProtocol
FormatJSON, XML, text, others (usually JSON)XML only (Envelope, Header, Body, Fault)
TransportHTTPHTTP, SMTP, others
EndpointsOne URL per resourceUsually one
MethodsGET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETEMostly POST to one endpoint
ContractOpenAPI/Swagger (optional)WSDL (required)
StateStatelessCan be stateful
CachingYesNo
SecurityHTTPS, OAuthWS-Security built in
WeightLight, fastHeavier, built-in transactions
Used inWeb and mobile apps (most modern apps)Banking, legacy enterprise

Tools: Postman for REST; SoapUI for SOAP.

cards.q: What data transfer formats do you know? JSON vs XML?
cards.a: JSON and XML are the main ones; others are YAML, CSV and Protobuf. JSON is made of key-value pairs, with strings, numbers, booleans, null, objects and arrays. It's compact and easy to read. XML uses opening and closing tags with attributes; it's more verbose but supports schemas for strict validation, and SOAP uses it.
cards.d:
JSON: lighter, easy to read, native to JS. Data types: string, number, boolean, null, object, array. XML: more verbose, opening/closing tags, attributes, namespaces, validated by XSD schemas; used by SOAP.

{"user": {"id": 42, "name": "Ann", "active": true, "tags": ["qa","lead"], "manager": null}}
<user id="42"><name>Ann</name><active>true</active></user>

cards.q: What is Swagger / the OpenAPI Specification?
cards.a: OpenAPI is a standard format, in YAML or JSON, for describing a REST API: its endpoints, parameters, request and response formats, and status codes. Swagger UI turns that file into interactive documentation where you can try requests. For a tester it's the main source of requirements for the API.
cards.d:
The OpenAPI file describes endpoints, parameters, schemas and responses. It's the tester's main source of truth for API requirements.

Try it: open petstore.swagger.io, expand an endpoint, press "Try it out" and execute.

cards.q: How do you test an API? What do you check?
cards.a: First I check that the status code is correct for each case, for example 200 or 201 for success, 400 for bad data and 404 for a missing resource. Then the response body: values, data types, required fields and the JSON schema. Then headers, like Content-Type. I run negative cases: missing required fields, wrong types, too long values, invalid IDs. I check auth: no token gives 401, a wrong role gives 403. I run a CRUD chain: create, read, update, read, delete, and then read gives 404. I also check pagination, filters and sorting, response time, and that the data is really saved in the database.
cards.d:
• Status code is correct for each case (200/201/204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422).
  • Response body: values, data types, required fields, JSON schema.
  • Headers: Content-Type, caching, CORS.
  • Negative cases: missing required fields, wrong types, too long values, invalid IDs, extra fields.
  • Auth: no token → 401, wrong role → 403, expired token.
  • CRUD chain: create → read → update → read → delete → read gives 404.
  • Pagination, filters, sorting; idempotency; response time; data really saved in the DB.

cards.q: You test POST /users that creates a user. What do you check?
cards.a: First the happy path: valid data returns 201, the response body has the right fields and types, and a GET confirms the user was saved. Then negative cases: missing fields, invalid formats, too-long values and a duplicate email should return 400 or 409 with clear messages, never a 500. Then auth: no token gives 401, no permission gives 403. Finally, headers, no password in the response, and response time.
cards.d: Also: send the same request twice and check for duplicates; empty body and broken JSON give 400.

cards.q: What is Postman, and what can you do in it?
cards.a: Postman is a tool for sending API requests and testing them. I can group requests into collections and folders, and use environments and variables, for example for the base URL and the token. It has auth helpers and pre-request scripts, and I can write tests in JavaScript, for example to check that the status is 200. The Collection Runner runs a collection with data files, and Newman runs it from the command line for CI. It also has mock servers and can import requests from Swagger or cURL.
cards.d: A tool for sending API requests and testing them. Collections and folders, environments and variables ({{baseUrl}}, {{token}}), auth helpers, pre-request scripts, tests in JS (pm.test("Status 200", () => pm.response.to.have.status(200))), Collection Runner with data files, Newman (CLI runner for CI), mock servers, import from Swagger/cURL.

cards.q: Path parameter vs query parameter?
cards.a: A path parameter is part of the URL path and identifies a resource. For example, in /users/42 the 42 is a path parameter: it means the user with ID 42. A query parameter comes after the question mark and filters, sorts or paginates. For example, /users?role=qa and page=2 means only QA users, second page.
cards.d: Path parameter identifies a resource: /users/42. Query parameter filters, sorts or paginates: /users?role=qa&page=2.

cards.q: What authentication methods do you know?
cards.a: I know Basic auth, where the login and password go in a header in base64, so it's used only with HTTPS. Then an API key, and a Bearer token. OAuth 2.0 uses access and refresh tokens from an authorisation server, like Login with Google. JWT is a token with three parts: header, payload and signature. And there are session cookies. Also, authentication is who you are, and authorisation is what you're allowed to do.
cards.d: Basic (base64 login:password in a header, only with HTTPS), API key, Bearer token, OAuth 2.0 (access + refresh tokens via an authorisation server, "Login with Google"), JWT (header.payload.signature, base64url, you can decode the payload on jwt.io), session cookies. Authentication = who you are; authorisation = what you're allowed to do.

cards.q: What is GraphQL?
cards.a: GraphQL is a query language for APIs. It has one endpoint, and the client specifies exactly which fields it needs, so it avoids over-fetching and under-fetching. For testing, one important point: GraphQL usually returns 200 even when there are errors. The errors sit in an errors array in the body, so I check the body, not just the status code.
cards.d: A query language for APIs with one endpoint, where the client specifies exactly which fields it needs, avoiding over- and under-fetching. Usually returns 200 even with errors, which sit in an errors array, so you check the body, not just the status.

cards.q: What is a browser, and what does it consist of? Which engines?
cards.a: A browser is a program that requests web resources from servers and displays them. Its main parts are the user interface, the rendering engine that turns HTML and CSS into the page, the JavaScript engine that runs scripts, the networking part that sends requests, and storage for cookies, cache and local storage. Chrome and Edge use the Blink engine, Safari uses WebKit, and Firefox uses Gecko.
cards.d:
Chrome, Edge, Opera, Brave, Samsung Internet use Blink (JS engine V8). Safari uses WebKit (JavaScriptCore). Firefox uses Gecko (SpiderMonkey).

Why engines matter: different engines render CSS and run JS differently, so cross-browser bugs mostly appear between engines, so test at least one browser per engine.

On iOS, browsers have historically all been required to use WebKit (the EU now allows exceptions), so Chrome on iPhone behaves like Safari.

cards.q: How do you choose which browsers to test in?
cards.a: First from the requirements and the product's own analytics: which browsers the real users have. If there's no data, from market share statistics like StatCounter: Chrome first, then Safari, Edge and Firefox. I make sure every engine is covered, test the latest version and one previous, and include mobile browsers.
cards.d:
First the requirements and the product's analytics (who actually visits). Otherwise global/regional market share (StatCounter): Chrome first by far, then Safari (large because of iPhones), Edge, Firefox, Samsung Internet. Cover each engine, the latest and one previous version, desktop and mobile.

Criteria in one line: requirements → analytics → market share → engines → versions → desktop and mobile.

cards.q: What are DevTools? Which panels do you use, and for what?
cards.a: DevTools are the developer tools built into the browser, opened with F12. One: in Network I check requests, status codes and responses to see if a bug is frontend or backend. Two: in Console I look for JavaScript errors. Three: in Elements I inspect and edit HTML and CSS, for example to remove a field's length limit. Four: in Application I view and delete cookies and local storage. Five: I throttle the network to simulate a slow connection. Six: I use device mode to check mobile screen sizes.
cards.d:
• Elements: inspect and edit DOM/CSS live, check fonts, colours, sizes vs design; force :hover state; device toolbar for responsive (phone and tablet sizes).
  • Console: JS errors and warnings; run JS.
  • Network: every request: method, URL, status, headers, payload, response, timing; throttling; disable cache; preserve log; export HAR; copy as cURL; block requests.
  • Application: cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, cache, service workers; clear site data.
  • Sources: JS files, breakpoints, local overrides.
  • Performance / Memory: profiling. Lighthouse: performance, accessibility, SEO, best practices audit.

Used less often: Lighthouse for audits, Performance for slow pages, Sources for JavaScript.

  • Open: F12, or Ctrl+Shift+I / Cmd+Opt+I.
  • More: take a full-page screenshot.

Memory hook: Elements = what you see, Console = what broke, Network = what was sent, Application = what's stored.

Expect to be asked to show this live.

cards.q: How do you tell whether a bug is on the frontend or the backend?
cards.a: I open DevTools, go to the Network tab and reproduce the bug. I find the request that loads the data and check the request and the response. If the request is wrong, it's a frontend bug. If the request is correct but the response is wrong, it's backend. If the response is correct but the page shows it wrong, it's frontend again. I attach the request and response to the bug.
cards.d:
If the request sent is wrong (wrong parameters, missing field) → frontend. If the request is correct but the response is wrong (wrong data, 500) → backend. If the response is correct but the page shows it wrong → frontend. Attach request/response or a HAR file to the bug.

Example: cart shows $45, should be $27. Response says 45 → backend. Response says 27 but page shows 45 → frontend.

Also check the Console for JavaScript errors.

cards.q: What are cookies? What types and attributes do they have?
cards.a: Cookies are small pieces of data a website stores in the browser and that the browser sends back with every request to that site. They keep you logged in, remember settings and track visits. Session cookies disappear when the browser closes; persistent cookies have an expiry date. First-party cookies belong to the site you're on; third-party cookies belong to another domain, like an ad network.
cards.d:
• Attributes: Domain, Path, Expires / Max-Age, Secure (HTTPS only), HttpOnly (JavaScript can't read it), SameSite (limits cross-site sending).
  • Tests: delete the session cookie → logged out; cookie expires at the right time; the session cookie has Secure and HttpOnly; the cookie consent banner works.

cards.q: What is a HAR file?
cards.a: A HAR file is an HTTP Archive. It's a JSON log of all the network requests and responses with their timings, and I export it from the Network tab in DevTools. With it, developers can replay exactly what happened in my browser. I have to be careful with it, because it can contain cookies and tokens.
cards.d: HTTP Archive: a JSON log of all network requests and responses with timings, exported from the Network tab. Developers can replay exactly what happened in your browser. Be careful: it can contain cookies and tokens.

cards.q: Why use incognito / private mode in testing?
cards.a: I use incognito mode to get a clean state: there are no cookies, no cache, no logged-in sessions and, by default, no extensions. So I see the site exactly as a new user sees it. It's also handy when I need to test as two different users at the same time.
cards.d: Clean state: no cookies, cache, logged-in sessions or extensions (by default), so you see what a new user sees. Handy to test as two different users at once.

cards.q: What browser extensions are useful for QA?
cards.a: I use extensions for a few things. For checking the design: ColorZilla as a colour picker, WhatFont, and PerfectPixel to overlay the design on the page. For requests and data: Cookie-Editor, ModHeader to change headers, User-Agent Switcher and a JSON formatter. For test data: Bug Magnet or Fake Filler. For bug reports: full-page screenshots and screen recording, like Awesome Screenshot or Loom. And for accessibility: axe DevTools and WAVE.
cards.d: ColorZilla (colour picker), WhatFont, PerfectPixel (overlay design), page ruler / Dimensions, Window Resizer, Cookie-Editor, ModHeader (change headers), User-Agent Switcher, JSON formatter, Bug Magnet / Fake Filler (test data), Lorem ipsum generator, full-page screenshot and screen recording (Awesome Screenshot, Loom, Jam), axe DevTools and WAVE (accessibility), Wappalyzer (tech stack), VPN extensions.

cards.q: What is HTML? Basic structure of a page?
cards.a: HTML is HyperText Markup Language. It describes the structure and content of a page with elements, or tags, and attributes, and the browser turns it into the DOM tree. A basic page starts with the DOCTYPE, then the html element with two parts. The head holds the meta tags, the title and the link to the styles. The body holds the visible content, like header, main and footer, and the scripts.
cards.d:
HyperText Markup Language: describes the structure and content of a page with elements (tags) and attributes. The browser turns it into the DOM tree.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Shop</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="s.css"></head>
  <body><header>…</header><main>…</main><footer>…</footer><script src="app.js"></script></body>
</html>

cards.q: Which tags and attributes do you know?
cards.a: For structure I know div and span, p for paragraphs, h1 to h6 for headings, a for links, img for images, lists with ul, ol and li, and tables with table, tr and td. For forms: form, input, button, select, textarea and label. There are also semantic tags like header, nav, main, section, article and footer. Attributes I know: id, class, href, src, alt, type, name, value, placeholder, required, maxlength, pattern, disabled and data attributes.
cards.d: Tags: div, span, p, h1–h6, a, img, ul/ol/li, table/tr/td, form, input, button, select, textarea, label, semantic header, nav, main, section, article, footer. Attributes: id, class, href, src, alt, type, name, value, placeholder, required, maxlength, pattern, disabled, data-*.

cards.q: Block vs inline elements?
cards.a: Block elements, like div, p, h1 and ul, start on a new line and take the full width, and width and height apply to them. Inline elements, like span, a and strong, flow within the text and take only the width they need; width and height don't apply to them. There is also inline-block, which flows inline but accepts sizes.
cards.d: Block (div, p, h1, ul) start on a new line and take full width; width/height apply. Inline (span, a, strong) flow within text and take only needed width; width/height don't apply. inline-block flows inline but accepts sizes.

cards.q: What is CSS? How can it be added?
cards.a: CSS is Cascading Style Sheets. It describes how elements look: colours, fonts, spacing, layout and animations. There are three ways to add it: inline, in the style attribute of an element; internal, in a style tag on the page; and external, with a link to a separate CSS file, which is the usual way. Cascading means that rules combine and override each other by specificity and order.
cards.d: Cascading Style Sheets describe how elements look: colours, fonts, spacing, layout, animations. Added inline (style=""), internal (<style>) or external (<link> to a .css file, the usual way). "Cascading" = rules combine and override by specificity and order.

cards.q: CSS selectors and specificity?
cards.a: Selectors choose which elements a rule applies to. The main ones are tag, like p; class, with a dot; id, with a hash; attribute, in square brackets; descendant and child selectors; pseudo-classes like hover; and pseudo-elements like before. Specificity decides which rule wins. From strongest to weakest: important, then inline style, then id, then class, attribute and pseudo-class, then tag. If the weight is the same, the later rule wins.
cards.d: Selectors: tag p, class .btn, id #login, attribute [type="email"], descendant form input, child ul > li, pseudo-class :hover, :nth-child(2), pseudo-element ::before. Specificity (strongest first): !important > inline style > id > class/attribute/pseudo-class > tag. Same weight → the later rule wins.

cards.q: What is the box model?
cards.a: Every element is a box with four layers, from the inside out: content, padding (space inside the border), border, and margin (space outside, pushing other elements away). Sizes add up, which causes layout bugs; box-sizing: border-box makes the width include padding and border.
cards.d:
content → padding (inside the border) → border → margin (outside, space to neighbours).

Framed photo: photo = content, matting = padding, frame = border, gap to the next frame = margin.

200px width + 10px padding each side + 1px border each side = 222px. Check it in DevTools → Elements → Computed, which shows it visually.

cards.q: display: none vs visibility: hidden?
cards.a: display none removes the element from the layout entirely, so it takes no space. visibility hidden hides the element but keeps its space, so an empty place stays where it was. There is also opacity zero: the element is invisible, it keeps its space, and it can still be clicked.
cards.d: display:none removes the element from layout entirely (no space). visibility:hidden hides it but keeps its space. opacity:0 keeps space and it can still be clicked.

cards.q: CSS position values?
cards.a: There are five values. Static is the default: the element stays in the normal flow. Relative moves it by an offset from its normal place. Absolute removes it from the flow and positions it relative to the nearest positioned ancestor. Fixed positions it relative to the viewport, so it stays in place on scroll. Sticky behaves normally until a scroll threshold and then sticks.
cards.d: static (default flow), relative (offset from its normal place), absolute (relative to the nearest positioned ancestor, removed from flow), fixed (relative to the viewport, stays on scroll), sticky (normal until a scroll threshold, then sticks).

cards.q: Units: px, %, em, rem, vw/vh?
cards.a: Pixels are absolute. Percent is relative to the parent. Em is relative to the element's font size, and rem is relative to the root font size. vw and vh are one percent of the viewport width and height. Related to this, media queries, for example max-width 768 pixels, switch styles for different screen sizes.
cards.d: px absolute; % of parent; em relative to the element's font size; rem relative to the root font size; vw/vh 1% of viewport width/height. Media queries (@media (max-width: 768px)) switch styles per screen size.

cards.q: Why does a QA engineer need HTML and CSS?
cards.a: The UI is HTML and CSS, so knowing them helps me test and report precisely. I inspect elements to compare fonts, colours and spacing with the design, write bug reports that point to the exact element and attribute, and edit the page in DevTools to test edge cases, like long text or removing maxlength to check server-side validation. It also helps with accessibility checks and writing locators for automation.
cards.d:
• Find elements and write precise bug reports ("button #submit has disabled attribute").
  • Compare fonts, colours, spacing with the design.
  • Test edge cases fast: edit text to a very long string, remove maxlength/required/disabled to check server-side validation.
  • Check accessibility basics: alt, label, heading order.
  • Write locators for automation: CSS selectors and XPath (//button[text()='Log in']).

"Errors manifest there" is the why; interviewers want the concrete how.

cards.q: Show how you find the request sent when the user logs in.
cards.a: I open DevTools and go to the Network tab. I tick Preserve log, because the page will redirect after login. I filter by Fetch/XHR, or by Doc if it's a form post. Then I log in and click the login request. In Headers I see the method, URL, status and the request and response headers; in Payload, what was sent; in Response or Preview, what came back. There are also Cookies and Timing tabs.
cards.d: Open Network → check "Preserve log" (page will redirect) → filter Fetch/XHR (or Doc for form posts) → log in → click the request → Headers (method, URL, status, request and response headers), Payload (what was sent), Response/Preview (what came back), Cookies, Timing.

cards.q: How do you emulate a slow network or offline mode?
cards.a: In DevTools I open the Network tab and use the throttling dropdown. I can choose Fast 4G, Slow 4G, 3G or Offline, or add a custom profile. Then I check how the app behaves: loaders, timeouts, error messages, and whether the same form can be submitted twice.
cards.d: Network tab → throttling dropdown → Fast 4G / Slow 4G / 3G / Offline, or add a custom profile. Check loaders, timeouts, error messages, double-submits.

cards.q: How do you test a page on mobile screen sizes in the browser?
cards.a: I open the device toolbar in DevTools with Ctrl or Cmd plus Shift plus M. There I pick a device preset or set a custom width, rotate the screen, set the device pixel ratio, and throttle the network. But it's only emulation: it changes the viewport and the user agent, not the browser engine. So real devices are still needed, especially for Safari on iOS.
cards.d: Device toolbar (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+M) → pick a device preset or set custom width, rotate, set DPR, throttle. It's emulation only: it changes viewport and user agent, not the engine, so real devices are still needed (iOS Safari especially).

cards.q: How do you check that the server validates input too?
cards.a: In the Elements panel I find the input and delete the attribute that limits it in the browser: maxlength, required, pattern or disabled. Then I submit invalid data. If the server accepts it, that's a bug. Another way is to edit and resend the request itself, using Copy as cURL or Postman.
cards.d: Elements → find the input → delete the maxlength, required, pattern or disabled attribute → submit invalid data. If the server accepts it, that's a bug. Or edit and resend the request with Copy as cURL / Postman.

cards.q: How do you find and clear cookies / storage for a site?
cards.a: I open the Application tab, then Storage, Cookies, and choose the site. There I see each cookie's name, value, domain, expiry and the HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite flags, and I can edit or delete them. Local storage and session storage work the same way. For a completely fresh start I use Clear site data, which wipes everything for that site.
cards.d: Application tab → Storage → Cookies → site: view name, value, domain, expiry, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite; edit or delete. Same for Local/Session storage. "Clear site data" wipes everything for a fresh start.

cards.q: How do you take a screenshot of the full page?
cards.a: I open the command menu in DevTools with Ctrl or Cmd plus Shift plus P and choose Capture full size screenshot. Another way is in device mode: the three-dot menu, then Capture screenshot. And if I need only one element, I right-click its node in the Elements panel and choose Capture node screenshot.
cards.d: Command menu Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P → "Capture full size screenshot". Or in device mode, ⋮ menu → Capture screenshot. Element screenshot: right-click node → Capture node screenshot.

cards.q: How do you get console errors for a bug report?
cards.a: I open the Console tab, filter by Errors, and reproduce the bug. Then I copy the error messages, or take a screenshot of them together with the stack trace link, and add that to the bug report. If the error is related to a failed request, I also mention that request from the Network tab.
cards.d: Console tab → filter Errors → reproduce → copy the messages or screenshot them with the stack trace link; mention the failing request from Network if related.

cards.q: What is a sniffer, and why do testers use it?
cards.a: A sniffer is a tool that captures network traffic. Charles and Fiddler are debugging proxies. They sit between an app and the server, so I can see every request and response. That's especially useful for mobile apps, which have no DevTools. I use them to tell frontend bugs from backend ones, and to change traffic to test edge cases: breakpoints to fake a 500 error, Map Local to return custom data, throttling to simulate a slow network.
cards.d:
HTTP debugging proxies (Charles, Fiddler, Proxyman, mitmproxy) work as a man-in-the-middle proxy between client and server. Testers use them to see requests from mobile/desktop apps (no DevTools there), find whether a bug is frontend or backend, modify requests and responses to test edge cases and error handling without backend changes, emulate slow networks, check analytics events, and point the app to another environment. Wireshark is a lower-level packet sniffer (all protocols), rarely needed for web QA.

App ⇄ Charles ⇄ Server.

Also: block a request to simulate a service being down.

Charles runs everywhere (paid, trial); Fiddler Classic is free on Windows.

cards.q: How do you set up Charles to capture traffic from a phone?
cards.a: First, the computer and the phone must be on the same Wi-Fi. In Charles I find the computer's local IP address; the proxy port is 8888. On the phone, in the Wi-Fi settings, I set a manual proxy with that IP and port, and I accept the connection prompt in Charles. Then, for HTTPS, I open chls.pro/ssl on the phone and install the Charles certificate; on iOS I also enable it in Certificate Trust Settings. Finally, I enable SSL Proxying in Charles for the host I need.
cards.d:
1. Computer and phone on the same Wi-Fi.
  2. In Charles: Help → Local IP address (e.g. 192.168.1.5); proxy port 8888.
  3. On the phone: Wi-Fi settings → Proxy → Manual → computer IP, port 8888.
  4. Accept the connection prompt in Charles.
  5. On the phone open chls.pro/ssl and install the certificate. iOS: also enable it in Settings → General → About → Certificate Trust Settings. Android 7+: apps trust user certificates only if the app's network security config allows it (usually debug builds).
  6. In Charles: Proxy → SSL Proxying Settings → enable and add *:443 or the specific host.

cards.q: Why do you install the Charles certificate to see HTTPS traffic?
cards.a: HTTPS encrypts the traffic, so Charles has to decrypt it as a man-in-the-middle and re-encrypt it with its own certificate. The device only accepts that if it trusts Charles's certificate. Without it, you'd see only encrypted traffic or get connection errors.
cards.d: You reasoned this out from the HTTPS question: a good way to handle unfamiliar questions.

cards.q: Why might HTTPS traffic not show even with the certificate installed?
cards.a: There are several possible reasons. SSL proxying may not be enabled for that host in Charles. The certificate may be installed but not trusted, for example in the iOS trust settings. On Android, the app may not trust user certificates; that needs a network security config in a debug build. The app may use certificate pinning, or ignore the system proxy. The traffic may not be HTTP, like WebSocket or gRPC. Or a VPN is active.
cards.d: SSL proxying not enabled for that host; the certificate not trusted (iOS trust settings); Android app doesn't trust user CAs (needs network security config in a debug build); certificate pinning in the app; the app ignores the system proxy; traffic isn't HTTP (e.g. WebSocket or gRPC needs extra setup); a VPN is active.

cards.q: What can you do with Breakpoints, Map Local, Rewrite, Throttling?
cards.a: Breakpoints pause a specific request or response so I can edit it on the fly, for example change the status to 500 or edit a price, and see how the app handles it. Map Local replaces a server response with a local file, so I can test the UI with any data, like an empty list or very long names. Rewrite is an automatic rule that changes headers, body, URL or status for matching requests. Throttling emulates a slow or unstable network, like 3G.
cards.d:
• Breakpoints: pause a specific request or response and edit it on the fly (change status to 500, edit a price, remove a field) to see how the app handles it.
  • Map Local: replace a server response with a local file. Test UI with any data (empty list, very long names, 1000 items).
  • Map Remote: redirect requests to another host (e.g. prod app → staging API).
  • Rewrite: automatic rules to change headers, body, URL or status for matching requests.
  • Throttling: emulate slow or unstable networks (3G, latency, packet loss).
  • Repeat / Compose: resend or craft a request; Block list: block a host to emulate a failed service.

cards.q: Charles vs Fiddler?
cards.a: They have the same purpose. Charles is written in Java and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux; it's paid, with a trial where sessions are limited to 30 minutes. Fiddler Classic is free but only for Windows, and Fiddler Everywhere is cross-platform with a subscription. The features are similar: Fiddler's AutoResponder is like Map Local in Charles, and Composer is like Compose. On macOS, Proxyman is a popular alternative.
cards.d: Same purpose. Charles: Java, macOS/Windows/Linux, paid with a trial (sessions limited to 30 min). Fiddler Classic: Windows, free; Fiddler Everywhere: cross-platform, subscription. Fiddler's AutoResponder ≈ Charles Map Local; Composer ≈ Compose. On macOS, Proxyman is a popular alternative.

cards.q: How do you find out whether a mobile app bug is client or server side?
cards.a: I capture the app's traffic in Charles while I reproduce the bug. Then I compare the request with the API specification, for example Swagger. If the request is wrong, it's a client bug. If the request is correct but the response is wrong, it's a server bug. If the response is correct but the app shows it wrong, it's a client bug again. I attach the request and response, or a Charles session file, to the bug report.
cards.d: Capture the traffic in Charles while reproducing. Compare the request with the API spec (Swagger): wrong request → client bug. Correct request, wrong response → server bug. Correct response shown wrong → client bug. Attach the request/response (or a Charles session file) to the bug report.

cards.q: What is cURL? Show a few commands.
cards.a: cURL is a command-line tool for sending HTTP requests. Testers use it for quick API checks, and especially to reproduce bugs: in DevTools I right-click a request, choose Copy as cURL, and put it in the bug report so the developer can rerun the exact request. It's also handy on servers where there's no UI. For example, curl with just a URL sends a GET request; with -X POST, -H for a header and -d for the data, I send a POST; and -i also shows the response headers.
cards.d:
A command-line tool to transfer data with URLs: send any HTTP request without a UI. Great for quick API checks, reproducing bugs exactly, and sharing requests with developers (DevTools → Copy as cURL).

cURL is a tool, not a type of request.

Flags: -X method, -H header, -d data, -i response headers, -v verbose, -L follow redirects.

curl https://api.shop.com/products/1
curl -X POST https://api.shop.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"Ann"}'
curl https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1          # GET
curl -i https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1       # include response headers
curl -I https://example.com                                # HEAD: headers only
curl -v https://example.com                                # verbose: TLS, request, response
curl -L http://github.com                                  # follow redirects
curl -X POST https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"qa","body":"hello","userId":1}'
curl -X DELETE https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1
curl -u user:passwd https://httpbin.org/basic-auth/user/passwd
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer abc123" https://httpbin.org/bearer
curl -o page.html https://example.com                      # save to file

cards.q: Write a cURL POST with a JSON body and an authorization header. Explain each part.
cards.a: curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" -d '{"name":"Ann"}'. The -X flag sets the method, each -H adds a header, and -d is the request body. Adding -i shows the response headers and status code.

Flags to know:

FlagMeaning
-XHTTP method
-HAdd a header
-dRequest body (data)
-iShow response headers
-ISend HEAD: headers only
-vVerbose: full request and response
-LFollow redirects
-uuser:password (basic auth)
